slides.title: The outcomes this session serves
slides.sub: One course outcome, four chapter objectives

items.head: LO-3
items.body: Build, configure and run Bitcoin Core as a full node, verify the release before trusting it, and query the node over its JSON-RPC interface to inspect blocks, transactions and the state of the chain.

rows: What you should be able to do after this session
Decode a transaction by hand: compute its txid, hash, weight and virtual size from its serialization
Explain what a full node verifies and why Bitcoin Core's own answers are authoritative
Choose and justify Bitcoin Core options, such as prune, txindex and dbcache, for a given machine
Recompute a block's Merkle root and header hash, and check a printed result against the software and the chain

slides.notes: Read the course outcome aloud and say which part of it this chapter reaches. The chapter's objectives are the page's own and are what the question bank and the mock exam are written against. Course outcome LO-3 is recorded as a draft that the course owner has not yet approved, so present it as the direction of the course rather than as a settled requirement.

slides.title: The questions this chapter answers

items: Which programs does Bitcoin Core consist of, how is each obtained, built and started, and what does the project's documentation say about each?
Which settings and files decide how a node runs, how much it stores and how it protects its interface, and what does each hold in release 31.1?
Which numbers does the node report about a transaction and a block, and how can each be recomputed from the bytes?
Where do the book's printed outputs differ from the real release 31.1 and the current source, and what does each difference change?
How can a downloaded release and a chosen library be checked before they are trusted, and what does each check not prove?

slides.notes: These are the competency questions the chapter's ontology was written to answer, so they are a fair statement of what a student should be able to answer at the end. Come back to them in the recap. A student who can answer all of them has the chapter; a student who can answer none of them has memorised vocabulary.

slides.title: Node
slides.sub: A node is a computer that runs Bitcoin software and takes part in the peer-to-peer network, and this first branch of the chapter is about the most complete kind of node, the full verification node.
slides.notes:
The branch matters because it decides whom a user has to trust. The book explains that Bitcoin was designed so that software running entirely on your own computer can prevent counterfeiting, debasement and several other critical problems, and that the data such a node reports is authoritative not because a powerful entity designated it as such but because the node independently verified it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Every later chapter of the course examines transactions, blocks and mining, and it does so through the data that a node of this kind provides, so the branch is the practical foundation for everything that follows.

A full node is a choice with costs, and it should not be confused with other roles. It is not a miner, because it does not need to produce blocks; it is not necessarily a wallet, although Bitcoin Core includes one; and it is not the only implementation of the protocol, as the last branches of the chapter show. Running a node also does not remove every kind of trust, because a user still has to trust the software that was downloaded, which is why the ecosystem branch returns to the verification of releases.

slides.title: Verification

items.head: What this section covers
items.body: Verification is the second level of the node branch and gathers four ideas: the full node itself, the reference implementation, the Bitcoin Improvement Proposals and the soft fork. Together they answer one question, which is how a participant can be sure that what the software enforces is what the Bitcoin system actually requires. The first concept names the program that checks the rules, the second names the program that serves as the model of how to check them, and the last two explain how the written rules are documented and how they are changed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
The sections of the group move from the program to the rules. The full node verifies every confirmed transaction.

slides.notes:
Checking rules is only meaningful if everyone checks the same rules. A node that accepted a payment which the others rejected would be living on a different version of the money. For that reason the group does not stop at describing a program; it also describes the documents, the Bitcoin Improvement Proposals, in which the design of each major part of the system is written down, and the mechanism, the soft fork, by which the rules can be tightened while old and new nodes stay on the same chain.

Concepts in this section: Full node, Reference implementation, Bitcoin Improvement Proposal, Soft fork.

slides.title: Full node and Reference implementation

items.head: Full node
items.body: A full node, which the chapter introduces as a full verification node, is software that verifies every confirmed Bitcoin transaction against every rule in the system (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A full node receives blocks and transactions from its peers and checks each of them against the consensus rules, which chapter 2 listed for transactions: the syntax and data structure must be correct, the lists of inputs and outputs must not be empty, the amounts must be within the allowed range, the outputs being spent must exist and be unspent, the inputs must cover the outputs, and the scripts must validate (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

items.head: Reference implementation
items.body: A reference implementation is a program that serves as the model of how a specification should be realised. The book calls Bitcoin Core the reference implementation of the Bitcoin system, meaning that it provides a reference for how each part of the technology should be implemented, and it lists what Bitcoin Core implements: wallets, a transaction and block validation engine, tools for block construction, and all modern parts of the peer-to-peer communication (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.notes:
The reason for verifying everything is trust. The book states that the Bitcoin system was designed so that software on your own computer can perfectly prevent counterfeiting and debasement, and it describes the data that your own node returns as authoritative because your node independently verified it, whatever any powerful entity may say (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A user who relies on someone else's server to say that a payment has arrived has to trust that server. A user who relies on a full node has only to trust the software and the rules, and the rules are public.

Verifying every rule has a price that the chapter states openly: processing more than 500 GB of data at first and about 400 MB of new transactions a day, in the book's figures for 2023 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A full node also does not make a user's money safe by itself, because the wallet that holds the keys is a separate function, and it does not make a user a miner. Finally, the word full is not a promise about storage: a pruned node, described in the resource group, still verifies the whole chain but keeps only the most recent blocks.

---

A decentralized network needs participants who agree exactly on what is valid, and agreement is easier when a complete, running program exists that others can compare themselves with. The point is made by the source code itself: the constant that limits the total amount of money is annotated in Bitcoin Core with the remark that its exact value is consensus critical (Bitcoin Core, 2026). If two implementations differed even slightly on a rule of this kind, a block that one accepted could be rejected by the other, which is why the implementation that most nodes run carries so much weight.

Reference does not mean that the code is the specification. The book points out that the whitepaper describes several early parts of the system and that most major parts since 2011 are documented in Bitcoin Improvement Proposals, so the written documents and the code together describe the rules (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It also does not mean that Bitcoin Core is the only implementation: the final section of the chapter lists libraries, toolkits and full-node implementations in many languages, and the book's chapter on the network says that the most common implementation is Bitcoin Core, run by more than 95 per cent of the full nodes, which makes it dominant but not unique (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A learner should treat Bitcoin Core as the most widely used model and not as the only possible one.

slides.title: Bitcoin Improvement Proposal and Soft fork

items.head: Bitcoin Improvement Proposal
items.body: A Bitcoin Improvement Proposal, abbreviated BIP, is a design document providing information to the Bitcoin community or describing a new feature for Bitcoin or its processes or environment, in the words of the process document that governed BIPs from 2016 (Dashjr, 2016).

items.head: Soft fork
items.body: A soft fork is a change to the consensus rules that is backward compatible.
BIP 9 reinterprets the version field of a block as a bit vector in which each bit can track an independent change.

slides.notes:
The documents make the design of a decentralized system discussable. The process document says that BIPs are intended as the primary mechanisms for proposing new features, for collecting community input on an issue, and for documenting the design decisions that have gone into Bitcoin, and that the author is responsible for building consensus within the community and documenting dissenting opinions (Dashjr, 2016). Because the documents are text files in a versioned repository, their revision history is the historical record of the proposal. Without such a record, a rule would exist only as a line in somebody's code.

A BIP is a recommendation, not a decree. BIP 3 says in so many words that BIPs do not define what Bitcoin is: individual BIPs do not represent community consensus or a general recommendation for implementation, some may never be adopted, and no formal or informal decision body governs Bitcoin development or decides adoption (Murch, 2025). A document with the status Deployed has been implemented and activated; a document that exists in the repository has only been published. When the course cites a BIP, it cites it for the description of a mechanism, and the number is the stable name by which any reader can find the same text.

---

The advantage is that the network can be upgraded without splitting. Because older nodes still accept everything that newer nodes accept, an upgrade does not force every participant to move on the same day. The cost is coordination: the miners who produce the blocks and the nodes that enforce the rules have to agree when the new rule applies. The earlier methods of signalling support in the block version, as BIP 90 recounts, used thresholds of 75 and 95 per cent of the last 1000 blocks (Daftuar, 2016), and they allowed only one change to be rolled out at a time (Wuille et al., 2015).

A soft fork is backward compatible only for nodes that do not need to understand the new rule. Older nodes keep accepting blocks, but they no longer verify the new rule themselves, so a user who wants the full protection has to upgrade. The mechanism of signalling is also not a vote of the users: BIP 9 tallies the blocks that miners produce, and the nodes that enforce the rule decide which chain they will accept. The details of how a rule change is chosen and activated belong to the later chapters on mining and on the network.

slides.title: The Bitcoin Core project

items.head: What this section covers
items.body: The project group describes where Bitcoin Core comes from and who maintains it. It contains two concepts: open-source software, which is the legal and social form in which the program is published, and Satoshi Nakamoto, the name under which the system was first described and its first software written. Both belong to the first section of the chapter, From Bitcoin to Bitcoin Core, which explains why the program is called what it is (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The group first states the form of publication, with the license that allows anyone to use, change and pass on the code, and the community process by which changes are reviewed and released. It then turns to the…

slides.notes:
A student who meets the term full node soon asks who decides what the node software does. The answer given by the chapter is that nobody owns it in the ordinary sense. The source code is available under an open license, it is developed by an open community of volunteers, and it began as the work of a single person. Knowing this explains why the chapter can invite the reader to download the code, build it and even contribute to it, and why the book can treat the program as a public reference and not as a product.

Concepts in this section: Open-source software, Satoshi Nakamoto.

slides.title: Open-source software

items.head: What it is
items.body: Open-source software is software whose source code is available to everyone under a license that allows use, modification and redistribution. The Open Source Initiative, whose definition is widely used, says that open source does not just mean access to the source code: the distribution terms must also allow free redistribution, must include the source code, and must allow modifications and derived works (Open Source Initiative, 2026).

items.head: Where you meet it
items.body: The source files of Bitcoin Core that were read for this chapter state their terms in the header, with the sentence that the file is distributed under the MIT software license, and the readme repeats that Bitcoin Core is released under the terms of the MIT license (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The license text itself is short.

slides.notes:
Openness is what makes it reasonable to trust a program that guards money without trusting its authors. Anyone can read the code, compile it and test it, and the project's own readme asks for exactly that: testing and code review are the bottleneck of development, and because this is a security-critical project, a mistake might cost people lots of money, so changes should be tested by somebody other than the developer who wrote them (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book also draws a social consequence. Bitcoin is developed by an open community of volunteers, which by 2023 had more than 1,000 contributors, about a dozen developers working on the code almost full time and several dozen more part time, and it adds that anyone can contribute, including the reader (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Open source does not mean that the code has no defects, or that no one is in charge of releases. The license says plainly that the software is provided as is, and the readme warns that the master branch is not guaranteed to be stable (Open Source Initiative, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Openness of the source also does not by itself prove that a downloaded program was built from that source. For that reason the ecosystem branch of this chapter explains how a release is checked by its checksums and signatures and why some builds are made reproducible.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Satoshi Nakamoto

items.head: What it is
items.body: Satoshi Nakamoto is the name used by the person or people who designed Bitcoin and created its original reference implementation.

The chapter on the history of Bitcoin explains what Nakamoto combined: several prior inventions, such as digital signatures and Hashcash, into a completely decentralized electronic cash system that does not rely on a central authority for currency issuance or for the settlement and validation of transactions.

slides.notes:
The paper is the starting point of the technology. Its abstract proposes a solution to the double-spending problem using a peer-to-peer network, in which the network timestamps transactions by hashing them into an ongoing chain of hash-based proof of work, forming a record that cannot be changed without redoing the proof of work (Nakamoto, 2008). The chapter adds a fact about the order of events: the software was mostly completed before the whitepaper was published, because Nakamoto wanted to make sure that the implementation worked before publishing a paper about it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Two points should not be overstated. The first is authority: the book states that Nakamoto withdrew from the public in April 2011, leaving the development of the code and the network to a group of volunteers, and that neither Nakamoto nor anyone else exerts individual control over the system, which operates on transparent mathematical principles, open-source code and consensus among participants (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The second is identity: nothing in the sources of this course identifies the person or people behind the name, and a claim about the identity would need evidence that this course cannot give.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Node resources

items.head: What this section covers
items.body: Node resources are the things that a node consumes in order to do its work: time and bandwidth to download the chain, disk space to store it, memory to keep the data it needs often, and network connections to other nodes. The section Running a Bitcoin Core Node of the chapter lists the costs openly before it explains why a reader might still want to bear them, and this group collects the concepts needed to understand those costs (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
Four concepts make up the group. The initial download is the first synchronization with the network. A pruned node keeps only the recent blocks.

slides.notes:
The costs decide who can run a node, and therefore how widely the verification of the rules is spread. The book's figures for 2023 are over 500 GB of data to download and process at first, about 400 MB of transactions per day, at least 1 TB of disk if all transactions are indexed and the full copy is kept for several years, and upload bandwidth that a metered connection may not afford (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The current download page of Bitcoin Core states a one-time download of about 600 GB plus a further 5 to 10 GB per month, and says that with pruning a node can store as little as 10 GB (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Every option that lowers these costs, such as pruning, is a trade between cost and what the node can offer to others.

Concepts in this section: Initial download, Pruned node, Peer and connection, Set of unspent outputs.

slides.title: Initial download and Pruned node

items.head: Initial download
items.body: The initial download is the first synchronization of a new node with the network, in which it fetches the whole chain of blocks from its peers and validates every transaction in them.
The same arithmetic applies after any interruption.

items.head: Pruned node
items.body: A pruned node is a full node that deletes old block files after it has verified them, so that it needs far less disk space.

Bitcoin Core stores blocks in numbered files of 128 MiB each and deletes whole files until the stored blocks fit under the target, never touching the files that hold the 288 most recent blocks; the block index and the chain state are separate databases and stay (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

slides.notes:
The download is what turns the claim that a node verifies everything into a fact about a particular computer. Until the node has processed every block, it cannot know the current set of unspent outputs, so it cannot tell whether a payment is valid. The cost is substantial, and the book says it will take some time, perhaps more than a day, for the program to catch up to the current height, with almost a billion transactions to validate at the time of writing (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). That is the reason the chapter asks readers to make sure they have enough disk space, bandwidth and time before they begin.

The download is only the first of two jobs: the node must also validate what it fetches, and on slow hardware validation, not bandwidth, can be the bottleneck. Bitcoin Core's own documentation warns that when the system starts swapping memory pages to disk continuously, a node can slow to a crawl, especially during the initial synchronization, and that a lower database cache makes the initial synchronization much longer (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A learner should therefore treat the figures in the book as a snapshot of 2023 and not as a promise, and should check the current ones on the download page before planning a node.

---

Pruning allows a verifying node on a small machine. The current download page says that with pruning enabled a node can store as little as 10 GB in total without sacrificing any security (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The reason is that verification needs the current state of the chain and a recent stretch of blocks, not every old block: the node checked the old blocks when it first received them and keeps the compact record of unspent outputs, which is the basis for checking new ones. The price is that the node can no longer hand old blocks to other nodes.

Pruning cannot be undone cheaply. The help text warns that reverting the setting requires re-downloading the entire blockchain, and that wallets and indexes should be kept active while pruning is enabled so they stay synchronized before old block data is deleted (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A pruned node also cannot look up an old transaction or block that it has deleted, so the tools of this chapter, such as retrieving an arbitrary transaction by its identifier, work only for data that is still stored or that is part of the wallet. For a learner the safe rule is that pruning saves disk space and nothing else: it neither weakens verification nor makes the node faster.

slides.title: Peer and connection
slides.sub: a node connected to my node

items.head: What it is
items.body: A peer is another node of the Bitcoin network to which a node keeps a connection in order to exchange blocks and transactions. The chapter introduces the word when it says that, by default, Bitcoin nodes transmit transactions and blocks to other nodes, called peers, which consumes upload bandwidth (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A node finds peers from a stored list: the log of the book says that it loaded 63866 addresses from the file peers.dat, and the data directory of a node holds that file next to a list of banned addresses (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

slides.notes:
Peers are how a node learns about the world. It has no central server to ask, so every block and every unconfirmed transaction reaches it from a peer, and every block that it has verified is passed on in the same way. Chapter 2 described this spreading of data as gossiping. For the operator, peers are also a cost, since each active connection takes some memory and bandwidth, and a node on a metered connection may want to limit how much it uploads (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

A peer is not a trusted party. Everything it sends is checked by the receiving node against the rules, which is why a node can connect to strangers at all. The number of connections is also not a measure of quality: the node in the evidence files, started with its connections disabled, reports connections 0 and still holds a correct chain of one block (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Finally, the value of the default maximum differs between the release the book printed, release 31.1 and the newest source tree, so a configuration that depends on it should state the number explicitly.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Set of unspent outputs

items.head: What it is
items.body: The set of unspent outputs, in the chapter often called the UTXO set, is the collection of all transaction outputs that have been created and not yet spent.

items.head: How it works
items.body: Each block changes the set in the same way as the transaction of the example: the outputs that its transactions spend leave, and the new outputs enter.

slides.notes:
The set is what makes verification fast. To decide whether a new transaction is valid, a node does not need to search the whole history: it needs to know whether each output being spent is in the set. The chapter's checklist for transactions says that the outputs being spent must match outputs in the memory pool or unspent outputs in a block of the main branch (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The set is much smaller than the chain of blocks, because every spent output has left it.

The set is derived data, not part of any block, and every node builds it for itself by verifying the chain; two honest nodes get the same set only because they apply the same rules. It is also not a list of balances: the set holds outputs, and the amount a wallet owns is the sum of the outputs it can spend. Finally, the size of the set affects the memory a node needs, which is why the chapter lists the database cache among the options that a resource-constrained node should lower.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Build
slides.sub: The build branch is about turning the text of Bitcoin Core into a program that can run.
slides.notes:
Building from source is the most direct way to know what a node is made of. The source code of Bitcoin Core is public, so a reader who builds it has a program that corresponds to a particular version of the text that anyone can inspect, and can switch features on or off during the build, for example by leaving out the wallet. For a course on software engineering the branch also shows how a large, long-lived project organizes its work: a version control system, numbered releases, a build system that discovers what a computer provides, and an automatic test suite (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The most important caution is that the commands of the printed chapter belong to a build system that has been replaced: release 29.0 migrated the build from Autotools to CMake, and the current tree has a top-level CMakeLists.txt and no autogen.sh (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A student who follows the book literally on a current source tree fails at the first command. The second caution is that compiling it yourself does not prove that the program is trustworthy; it shows only that a program was built from the text you chose, and the choice of that text is made by selecting a release tag.

slides.title: Source

items.head: What this section covers
items.body: The source group contains the concepts needed to obtain the right text of the program: the source code itself, the Git repository in which the project keeps it, the release tag that names a particular stable version, and the release candidate that precedes it. The book teaches these in its sections on compiling Bitcoin Core from the source code and on selecting a release (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
The sections of the group follow the order of the commands in the chapter.

slides.notes:
The program changes every day, and not every day's version is safe to run. The book explains that by default the local copy of the repository is synchronized with the most recent code, which might be an unstable or beta version of Bitcoin (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The concepts of the group give a learner the means to say exactly which version is meant: a repository holds every version, a tag names one of them, and a suffix tells whether it is meant for testing.

Concepts in this section: Release tag, Source code, Git repository, Release candidate.

slides.title: Release tag and Source code

items.head: Release tag
items.body: A release tag is a name that the developers attach to one specific snapshot of the code repository in order to mark a release by its version number (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
The tag names a commit, the repository's own identifier of a snapshot.

items.head: Source code
items.body: Source code is the text in which a program is written, in a programming language that a person can read, before it is translated into the form that a computer executes. The book says that Bitcoin Core's source code can be downloaded as an archive or by cloning the source repository from GitHub (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
From the text to the program takes the steps of the build branch: a compiler translates each source file, a linker combines the results with libraries, and the build system orchestrates the order.

slides.notes:
Tags solve the problem of the moving target. The project's readme explains that the master branch is regularly built and tested but is not guaranteed to be completely stable, and that tags are created regularly from release branches to indicate new official, stable release versions (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A tag therefore lets two people on different continents talk about exactly the same code, and a book can say which version its screenshots belong to.

A tag is a label, not a guarantee. Checking out a tag gives the code that the maintainers tagged, but it does not by itself show that the label was placed by them, and the book's state message warns that the user is now in a detached HEAD state, where changes belong to no branch (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The tag list also contains names that follow no release scheme, such as noversion and v0.1.6test1. Trust in a release comes from the signatures and the reproducible builds described in the ecosystem branch.

---

The source is the only complete and exact description of the rules that the node enforces. The whitepaper describes several early parts of the system and the proposals describe later ones, but a question such as how much new money a block may create is answered finally by reading the code. The function GetBlockSubsidy in the file validation.cpp is a short example: it divides the block height by the halving interval, returns zero when the shift would be undefined, and otherwise starts from 50 coins and shifts the amount right by the number of halvings (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Reading the source requires care. The master branch holds work in progress, and a source file read at one commit can differ from the behavior of the release that a user runs, so a statement about the software should name the version it refers to. Also, a program that is open to reading is not thereby correct: the project's readme says that testing and review are the bottleneck and that every mistake might cost people lots of money, which is the reason the project asks for review by someone other than the author (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

slides.title: Git repository

items.head: What it is
items.body: Git is a distributed version control system, and a repository is the database in which it keeps a project and all of its history. The book calls Git the most widely used distributed version control system and an essential part of the toolkit of every software developer (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

items.head: How it works
items.body: Git names each snapshot, called a commit, by a hash computed from its content.

slides.notes:
A repository gives a project a memory and a way to share it. Because every copy contains the whole history, anyone can work offline, compare any two versions and verify that a given version is the one that the maintainers named. The chapter uses exactly this: the command git clone makes a complete local copy of the repository from GitHub, after which the command git tag shows the available release names, and the book's example output counts 245,912 objects received, about 217.74 MiB of data (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Two misunderstandings are common. A repository is not the same as a hosting service: GitHub stores a copy, and the clone on a user's machine is as complete as the original. And a clone is a snapshot of one moment, not a live view: the highest release at the time of writing was v24.0.1, whereas the public repository now holds the releases up to v31.1 and hundreds of tags in all, so a reader who cloned in 2023 does not see the later releases without updating the clone. The detached HEAD state that the book prints after checking out a tag is normal for reading a release and is a warning only for those who intend to commit changes.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Release candidate

items.head: What it is
items.body: A release candidate is a version that the developers believe could become the next stable release, published so that it can be tested first.

rows: [t for t in ['v0.11.2', 'v0.11.2rc1', 'v0.12.0rc2'] if 'rc' not in t]

items.head: How it works
items.body: Candidates are numbered in the order in which they are published: rc1, then rc2, rc3 and so on until a candidate is accepted and the same code is tagged without a suffix.

slides.notes:
The two-step method lets the project find problems before ordinary users depend on the software. For a program that guards money, the cost of a defect is high, and the project's readme stresses the need for testing by people other than the developers (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book's rule for readers follows: when selecting a release for compilation, choose the highest version without a suffix, because that is the one meant for production (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The suffix is a convention and not a guarantee, and not every unusual tag is a candidate: the first entries of the list include v0.1.6test1, which uses a different suffix. A candidate may also change before the final release, so results that a student obtains from a candidate need not hold for the release. The book itself recommends the plain tag, and a production system should follow that advice.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Toolchain

items.head: What this section covers
items.body: The toolchain group gathers the programs and conventions that turn source code into running executables: the build system, which decides how, the compilation, which does the translation, the prerequisites, which must be present, and the executables, which are the result.
The six concepts of the group fall into two sets.

slides.notes:
A build system exists because a large program is not compiled by one command. Bitcoin Core consists of many source files, depends on libraries that differ between computers, and offers options such as leaving out the wallet. The build system looks at the computer, records the choices, and runs the translation steps in the right order and, if interrupted, from where they stopped. Knowing the toolchain also explains why the same program can be obtained in several ways with the same result.

Concepts in this section: Autotools build, CMake build, The bitcoin command, Compilation, Build prerequisite, Executable, Package manager.

slides.title: Autotools build

items.head: What it is
items.body: Autotools is the family of tools with which Bitcoin Core was built until release 29.0, and the build of the book follows its three typical commands. The first, the script autogen.sh, creates a set of automatic configuration scripts that interrogate the system to discover the correct settings and make sure that all the necessary libraries are present. The second, configure, applies them and creates a customized build script for the computer. The third, make, runs the build (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

items.head: Where you meet it
items.body: The commands in the chapter are ./autogen.sh, ./configure --help, ./configure, make, make check and sudo make install, in this order, and the book shows output such as the lines beginning CXX that name the object file produced for each source file (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.notes:
The method was designed to make a program portable between operating systems without hand-editing. The script configure offers options that override the defaults, and the book lists four: --prefix, which overrides the installation location /usr/local, for example with $HOME on a computer where only the home directory is writable; --disable-wallet, which disables the reference wallet; --with-incompatible-bdb, which allows an incompatible version of the Berkeley DB library when building a wallet; and --with-gui=no, which leaves out the graphical interface that needs the Qt library (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The commands of this section no longer work on the current source. The top level of the current tree has no autogen.sh and no configure script, and the option --with-incompatible-bdb has lost its purpose since legacy BerkeleyDB wallets can no longer be created or loaded (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A learner should therefore read the Autotools section as an explanation of the structure of a build, with configure, compile, test and install, and use the CMake commands for any real work.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: CMake build

items.head: What it is
items.body: CMake is the build system that Bitcoin Core has used since release 29.0.

items.head: How it works
items.body: The build is divided into configuration and construction. The first command creates a build tree, the directory named after the -B option, in which CMake writes its cache with the chosen options. The second command builds the targets in that directory with whatever native tool is behind it.

slides.notes:
Moving the project to CMake replaced a collection of generated scripts by a description that works on the platforms the project supports. The release notes list what a user of the old method must change: the minimum required CMake version is 3.22, options are now given as CMake variables, and some defaults changed. For example, one now needs -DWITH_ZMQ=ON to build with the ZeroMQ messaging library and -DBUILD_GUI=ON to build the graphical client bitcoin-qt (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Copying options from a book or a blog is the usual source of failure. The names are specific to the build system and the version: an option written for Autotools is silently useless to CMake, and the build notes warn that the memory requirement is at least 1.5 GB for compiling, with advice on reducing it for smaller machines (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Environment variables that the old build honored, such as CXXFLAGS, have corresponding CMake variables with other names, so a build that is configured in a script needs to be rewritten, not merely adapted (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: The bitcoin command

items.head: What it is
items.body: The bitcoin command is a single program, introduced with release 30.0, through which the node and the other tools of Bitcoin Core are started. The installed-files table of the project describes it as the command-line tool for interacting with Bitcoin, which calls the other binaries (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The option -m, also written --multiprocess, makes the command run the multiprocess binaries bitcoin-node and bitcoin-gui, instead of the monolithic binaries bitcoind and bitcoin-qt, which are the default behavior.

slides.notes:
The command exists to hide a change in the structure of the software. The project plans to split Bitcoin Core into separate processes for the node, the wallet and the graphical interface, so that each can run in its own address space for better isolation. A front door that chooses the binary spares users from learning new names for each stage of that change (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

A beginner can confuse the new command with the old name. The word bitcoin by itself starts no node; it needs a command such as node. The multiprocess mode is experimental and, in the words of the release notes, the option -m is currently required for the mining interface but will become optional (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The chapter's examples are written with the older names and are still valid for the monolithic binaries.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Compilation and Build prerequisite

items.head: Compilation
items.body: Compilation is the translation of source code into executable machine code by a program called a compiler. The CMake manual defines the neighbouring notion of the buildsystem as the description of how to build a project's executables and libraries from its source code (Kitware, 2026).
The work is spread over many small jobs. Each source file is compiled independently into an object file, and a final step links the object files and the libraries into an executable.

items.head: Build prerequisite
items.body: A build prerequisite is a tool or library that must be installed on the computer before the program can be compiled. The book tells the reader to review the prerequisites, which it describes as the libraries that must be present on the system before the build can begin, in the first part of the build documentation, and adds that if they are missing the build process will fail with an error (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
Prerequisites are checked at configuration time.

slides.notes:
The step takes a long time and a lot of memory because the program is large. The book says that the compilation can take up to an hour depending on the speed of the processor and the available memory, and the build notes of the project recommend at least 1.5 GB of memory, with advice on reducing the demand, because C++ compilers are memory-hungry (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). These facts matter to an operator who plans a build on a small computer and to a student who wonders why the step cannot be skipped.

A successful compilation shows that the program was built, not that it behaves correctly, which is why the book tells the reader to run the unit test suite before installing (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Installing needs administrative privileges in the book's example, because the default installation location is /usr/local/bin; the book mentions installing to the home directory as the alternative where the computer does not allow it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

---

A large program is not written from nothing. Bitcoin Core relies on libraries for tasks such as storing the wallet in a database, drawing the graphical interface or sending messages to other programs, and each library has to be present in a version that fits. The documentation of dependencies exists so that a builder can see in advance what to install, and the book says that the build can be resumed from where it stopped after installing a missing prerequisite (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The prerequisites differ by platform and by release, so a list copied from a text about another system or version is likely to be wrong. The security perspective is that every library in the build is also part of the program that guards money, which is the reason the project documents the dependencies and offers a self-contained mechanism for building them, the depends system mentioned in its build notes (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

slides.title: Executable

items.head: What it is
items.body: An executable is a file that the operating system can run as a program. The book's installation step copies bitcoind, bitcoin-cli and bitcoin-tx into /usr/local/bin, and the command which asks the system for the path of an executable and confirms the installation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

items.head: Where you meet it
items.body: The release 31.1 archive that was downloaded and run for this chapter shows the layout: the folder bin holds bitcoin, bitcoin-cli, bitcoin-qt, bitcoin-tx, bitcoin-util, bitcoin-wallet and bitcoind, and the folder libexec holds bitcoin-gui, bitcoin-node and test_bitcoin (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

slides.notes:
Each executable has a separate purpose, so that a user can run the part that is needed. A server needs the node without a graphical interface; an operator who sends commands uses the client; a developer who builds a transaction offline uses the transaction tool. The book chooses to build the daemon, the server version, because the chapter is about a node running in the background (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The project's plan for the multiprocess design is that node, wallet and interface code run in separate address spaces for better isolation (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The name of an executable is not an interface guarantee. Names and places have changed between versions: the unit-test program test_bitcoin was moved from the folder bin to libexec in release 30.0, and the project advises starting multiprocess binaries through the bitcoin command and not directly (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A script that relies on a path should therefore state the release for which it was written.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Package manager
slides.sub: four package managers in the build notes

items.head: What it is
items.body: A package manager is the program of an operating system that installs, updates and removes software, together with the libraries each program needs, from a collection of packages.

rows:
t = '| Debian / Ubuntu (`apt`)
| Fedora (`dnf`)
| Alpine (`apk`)
| Arch (`pacman`)'

items.body: A package manager keeps a list of packages with their versions and their dependencies, and installs a package by installing everything it depends on first.

slides.notes:
Installing the prerequisites by hand would mean finding, downloading and compiling each library. A package manager does this with one command and resolves which other libraries are needed. The table of the build notes gives, for each system, the packages for the required build dependencies and then the optional ones for the wallet, the interprocess communication, the messaging and the graphical client, so that a builder chooses the columns that match the features wanted.

A package manager trusts the collection it installs from. The software the builder obtains is the software the maintainers of the distribution packaged, in the version they chose. For a security-critical program like a node, the project therefore also offers a way to build the dependencies from source, called depends in its notes (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Operation
slides.sub: Operation is the second large part of the chapter, and it is about what happens after the software has been built or downloaded: how a node is started, how it is configured, how its state is observed, and what kind of wallet comes with it.
slides.notes:
The branch matters because a node that is badly run gives little of what it promises. A node that is not given enough disk space cannot store the chain, a node whose cache is too small spends its time reading the disk, and a node whose settings nobody understands may expose services that were meant to stay private. The book lists the reasons for running a node in a short list: not relying on any third party to validate the transactions you receive, not disclosing to third parties which transactions belong to your wallet, having programmable access to the network and the blockchain, validating transactions according to the consensus rules in an application, and supporting the network (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Each of these reasons is only as good as the way the node is operated.

Two cautions apply to the whole branch. The first is that many of the book's figures belong to the release it printed: the default cache size, the wallet database and the first lines of the log differ in the current release, and the concepts of this branch give both values. The second is the warning in Bitcoin Core's own documentation, which tells users never to make configuration changes that they do not understand and to be wary of accepting any configuration changes provided to them by another source, even if they believe that they do understand them (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A copied configuration file is a set of instructions to a program that holds money-related data.

slides.title: Configuration

items.head: What this section covers
items.body: Configuration is the group of concepts that describe how a user tells Bitcoin Core how to behave.
The order of the concepts follows the order of the book.

slides.notes:
A node that runs on a default setting is usable, but the options are how it is adapted to the machine and to the purpose. The book's two sample files show the range: one is for a node that serves as the back end of a Bitcoin application and puts its data on a disk with a lot of room, the other is for a resource-constrained server and limits the cache, the mempool, the stored blocks and the traffic (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Knowing what each option does is what turns a copied example into a deliberate decision.

The options meet the reader in three forms: as lines of the configuration file, as parameters after the name of the program on the command line, and as entries in the help text, which the version 31.1 prints with 139 option entries, more than the hundred of the book (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The start-up messages of the node list the settings that it has actually read, so the log is the place where an option can be checked. The concepts that follow take the file, the option, the directory and then the individual settings.

Concepts in this section: Configuration file, Configuration option, Data directory, Database cache (dbcache), Transaction index (txindex), Blocks-only mode, Mempool limit (maxmempool), Alert notification (alertnotify).

slides.title: Configuration file

items.head: What it is
items.body: The configuration file is a plain text file, named bitcoin.conf by default, in which the owner of a node writes the options that the program should use.

items.head: How it works
items.body: The parser is simple. Blank lines are ignored, a comment starts with a number sign and runs to the end of the line, and a block with a name in square brackets, such as the one named main, holds options for one network only, which take precedence over options without a section (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

slides.notes:
A file is the practical way to keep a node's settings, because a node is meant to run for months and to restart after every power failure or update. The same options could be typed after the program name every time, but a file records them in one place that can be read, copied, compared and kept under control. It also keeps the settings out of the way of the start-up scripts that the book mentions in the end of the section, which only have to start the program (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Changes to the file take effect only after the node has been restarted, as the documentation states, so editing the file of a running node changes nothing until then (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The file is not a command language, and an option that the program does not know is not an error but shows up as a warning in the log, so a mistyped name can go unnoticed if nobody reads it. A last caution is that the file may hold secrets, for example the hashed credential of the interface, and should be readable only by the user who runs the node, which the init documentation also recommends for the file and the data directory (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Configuration option
slides.sub: dbcache on the command line and in the file

items.head: What it is
items.body: A configuration option is a named setting of the program, written in the book and in the help text with a leading hyphen, such as the setting that sets the size of the database cache.

items.head: How it works
items.body: The precedence can be shown with two dictionaries. The file says 450 for the cache and 1 for the transaction index; the command line says 2048 for the cache.

slides.notes:
The options are the program's interface for its owner, and the order in which their sources are read decides which value is used. The documentation states that all command-line options except the help, version and conf options may be specified in the configuration file, that all file options except the one that includes another file may also be given on the command line, and that command-line options override values set in the file (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A script that starts the node can therefore change one value for one run without editing the file.

The help text and the book must not be trusted blindly for the defaults, because defaults change from release to release: the book's value for the database cache is 450 and the current one is 1024 for machines with enough memory, and the minimum relay fee dropped in release 30.0 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Another common mistake is to put an option that is valid only on the command line, such as the one that names the file itself, into the file that it names, where it cannot work. A third is to forget that negation exists: a line written with the prefix no switches something off and is not a typing error.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Data directory

items.head: What it is
items.body: The data directory is the folder in which Bitcoin Core stores everything it has to remember between runs.

items.head: How it works
items.body: All content of the directory except the configuration file is specific to one network.

slides.notes:
The directory is the node's memory, so where it lives decides whether the node can run at all. The book says that, depending on the configuration, it can use from about 10 GB to almost 1 TB as of the writing, and that the maximum is expected to grow by several hundred gigabytes per year (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). For that reason the first sample file puts the directory on a separate disk with plenty of room, and a user who has a small system disk and a large second disk needs this option before the first start.

A directory is not a place to copy files from one running node to another. The documentation warns that a wallet file must not be shared across different node instances, because that can result in key reuse and double spends, and that a backup of a wallet should be made with the backup call so that the file is locked while it is copied (Bitcoin Core, 2026). It also advises against the exFAT filesystem on macOS, because of reports of database corruption (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The cheapest mistake, however, is to fill the disk: a node that cannot write stops, and that is the reason to plan the space.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Database cache (dbcache)

items.head: What it is
items.body: The database cache is a region of memory in which the node keeps part of the set of unspent outputs, so that it does not have to read the disk for every output it needs to check.

slides.notes:
The cache matters most while the node is catching up with the chain. The documentation on reducing memory says that a lower value makes the initial sync time much longer, and that after the first synchronization the effect is less pronounced for most uses, unless fast validation of blocks is important, such as for mining (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The same page warns that when the operating system starts swapping memory to disk continuously, the node can slow to a crawl, which is why a too-large value is also a mistake.

The memory is shared with the mempool, which the log shows by saying that up to 286.1 MiB of unused mempool space can be added to the 1014 MiB, a figure that the mempool limit concept explains (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Setting the value larger than the memory that is really available is a mistake that containers make easy, because the detected RAM may exceed what the container may use, a case that the release notes mention, and the node may then run out of memory (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The node also logs a warning when it believes a value is too large for the detected memory.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Transaction index (txindex) and Blocks-only mode

items.head: Transaction index (txindex)
items.body: The transaction index is an optional database that lets the node find any confirmed transaction by its identifier.

The source of the index describes it as written to a LevelDB database that records the block sequence number and the serialized block offset of each transaction by transaction hash (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

items.head: Blocks-only mode
items.body: Blocks-only mode is a setting in which the node does not take part in the relay of unconfirmed transactions.
In normal operation a node announces and requests unconfirmed transactions from its peers and keeps them in its mempool, from where it can tell a miner or a wallet about them.

slides.notes:
Without the index the node still has the whole chain, but it has no quick way from a transaction identifier to the block that holds it. The question matters to programs that look up arbitrary transactions, such as an explorer or the application back end of the book's first sample file. The book adds that if the option is not set at first and later set, one has to wait for the index to be rebuilt, and that the lookup works provided the block containing the transaction has not been pruned (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The index cannot be combined with pruning. The help text of the pruning option says the mode is incompatible with the transaction index, and the run of release 31.1 in the evidence confirms it: starting with both ends with the error that prune mode is incompatible with txindex (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The help of the current release is more exact than the book about what happens without the index: by default the call for a raw transaction returns a transaction only if it is in the mempool, and if the caller names a block, it returns the transaction when the block is available and contains it (Bitcoin Core, 2026). So a node without the index can still answer if it is told in which block to look, but not otherwise. Finally, the index is a convenience for the owner, and it is not part of the consensus rules.

---

The mode exists because relaying every transaction is the largest continuing cost of a node after the first download. A node in this mode still downloads and validates every block, so it enforces the same rules and remains a full node, but it receives each transaction only once, inside a block, and it holds no pool of unconfirmed transactions. The documentation on reducing memory says that the mode reduces the default memory use of the mempool to 5 MB, and that the source defines the blocks-only default as 5, against 300 for a normal node (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The mode has a privacy cost that the documentation spells out: it must not be used when the node is also used to broadcast transactions, because any transaction sent will stick out like a sore thumb, and when it is combined with the wallet, the wallet should be told not to broadcast and not to spend unconfirmed change, and another mechanism for broadcasting should be used (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Because such a node does not receive transactions that are not yet in a block, a merchant who wants to see a payment before its confirmation cannot rely on it.

slides.title: Mempool limit (maxmempool)

items.head: What it is
items.body: The mempool limit is the maximum size of the pool of unconfirmed transactions that the node holds, set by the option maxmempool. The book describes it as limiting the transaction memory pool to this many megabytes, and says to use it to reduce memory use on memory-constrained nodes; its second sample file sets it to 150 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The conversion explains the odd-looking figure: 300 megabytes is 300 times 10 to the sixth bytes, and dividing by 2 to the twentieth bytes per mebibyte gives 286.1 mebibytes, as the worked example computes.

slides.notes:
A pool that has no limit would let any sender fill the memory of every node with unconfirmed transactions. The limit forces the node to decide which transactions to keep, and the documentation says that a lower maximum means that transactions will be evicted sooner, which affects any use of the node that processes unconfirmed transactions (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Chapter 2 explained that a transaction waits in the mempool until it is mined; this is the bound on how long and how many can wait.

The unit is the usual mistake: a number of megabytes of 1000 bytes is smaller than the same number of mebibytes, and the two options that look alike, the mempool limit and the database cache, use different units. A node with a small mempool also forgets low-fee transactions sooner, so a wallet that depends on the node may see its payment dropped from that node's pool while other nodes still hold it. Bitcoin Core also expires transactions after a number of hours, an option that the help lists, so the limit is not the only bound.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Alert notification (alertnotify)

items.head: What it is
items.body: The alert notification is a hook that lets a node tell its owner that something is wrong.

rows: text = "'" + ''.join(c for c in msg if c in safe) + "'"

items.body: When a warning is set, the node calls a function that reads the command from the option, takes the warning text, strips every character that is not a letter, a digit, a blank or one of the characters in the string .,;-_/:?@(), puts single quotes around the result and replaces each %s in the command with it (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

slides.notes:
A node runs without anybody watching it, and some events need a person. Bitcoin Core's source shows two situations in which the node raises such a warning: when it finds an invalid chain with more work than its own best chain by more than six blocks of work, which could be due to database corruption or to consensus incompatibility with the peers, and when blocks signal new rules that this version of the software does not know, with the message that unknown new rules were activated and the number of the version bit (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Both are signs that the owner's software may be out of step with the network, a case that the soft fork concept explains.

The cleaning protects against the message but not against the owner's own script. A script that passes its argument on without quoting it can still be abused, and the %s must be inside the quotes of the command, as the book's sample does. The option also depends on the system providing a command interpreter, since the source compiles the function only if the system has one, and on the script being executable by the user who runs the node (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Finally, the command runs only when a warning is newly set, because the source calls it only if the warning was not already present, so a script that sends e-mail should not be the only way to learn that the node is in trouble.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Running

items.head: What this section covers
items.body: Running is the group of concepts that describe a node while it is alive: how it is started so that it keeps going without a person, what it writes while it starts, and how its owner asks two short questions about its state. The book moves from the configuration to this stage with a test: the node is started in the foreground with the option that sends the log to the console, the owner reads the lines to see whether the right settings are loaded, and interrupts the program once satisfied. Then the node is run in the background as a process and queried with the command line client (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
The concepts are taken in the order of events.

slides.notes:
A node is only useful when it runs continuously. The book ends the section with the advice to add Bitcoin Core to the start-up scripts of the operating system, so that it runs all the time and restarts when the operating system restarts, and it points to the examples in the folder contrib/init of the source (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The two status commands that follow tell the owner whether the node is synchronized with the chain and how it stands in the network, which are the two things that decide whether its answers can be relied on.

The reader meets this group the first time the program is started. The log printed to the console is the first thing seen, the data directory gains the log file and the files that mark a running process, and the owner types the first command to learn the state of the chain. The evidence of this version contains the real log of the release 31.1, the answers of its two status commands, and the directory it created, all from an offline node, which is a node that was told not to look for peers (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Concepts in this section: Daemon, Start-up log, Blockchain information (getblockchaininfo), Network information (getnetworkinfo).

slides.title: Daemon

items.head: What it is
items.body: A daemon is a program that runs in the background of the operating system, without a terminal and without a person typing to it, and waits for work.

rows: [w.split('=')[0] for w in line.split() if w.startswith('-') and not w.startswith('--')]

items.head: How it works
items.body: The systemd unit is a good example of what such a script does.

slides.notes:
The daemon form exists because a node has to run for months, through the closing of terminals and the restarting of machines. A program that is attached to a terminal ends when the terminal ends. For this reason the book advises to add the node to the startup scripts of the operating system, and the documentation of the project says that running the program as a daemon does not need any manual configuration, because it creates its own credential for the interface when it starts (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The sample scripts assume paths that may have to be adjusted, such as /usr/bin/bitcoind, /etc/bitcoin/bitcoin.conf and /var/lib/bitcoind, and a user and group called bitcoin that must be created before use (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The init documentation also says that datadir cannot be overridden in the configuration file with the init files as they are, because the command-line options in those files take precedence, and the comment at the top of the unit file says the same of every option named in its start command (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The operating system keeping a program alive does not mean it is healthy: a node that was restarted a hundred times because of a bad setting is still a node with a bad setting, and its log is where to look.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Start-up log

items.head: What it is
items.body: The start-up log is the stream of messages that the node writes while it starts, and afterwards as it runs.

rows: log = 'Starting HTTP server with 16 worker threads'
next(l for l in log.splitlines() if 'worker threads' in l).split()[-3]

items.head: How it works
items.body: Several lines can be compared with the book's log of release 24.0.1.

slides.notes:
Reading the log is how an owner checks what the node is really doing. The documentation of the configuration file says that the values in use can be seen in the log and that options in the file that the program does not recognize appear there as warnings, so a mistyped option is visible only to someone who reads it (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The log also records the environment the node found: the machine instructions used for hashing, the sources of randomness, the limits on connections and the memory it assigned to each cache.

The log is not a stable interface: the wording and the order of lines change from release to release, and a program that parses them breaks. It is also sensitive: the node itself warns that the log may hold privacy-sensitive information, so an owner who pastes a log into a public forum to ask for help should read it first. A last caution is about size: the help of the release has an option that shrinks the file at start-up, which is on by default when no debugging categories are selected, so an owner who wants a long history has to keep copies of the file himself.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Blockchain information (getblockchaininfo)

items.head: What it is
items.body: Blockchain information is the answer that the node gives to the call getblockchaininfo, the book's first example of monitoring a node: start it in daemon mode and then use the command bitcoin-cli getblockchaininfo to watch its progress and its status (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Some fields deserve a closer reading. The field with the work of the chain, written in hexadecimal, shows 100010001 at its end for the first block, as in the book's printout, which the chain work concept derives from the target.

slides.notes:
The answer is the quickest way to learn whether a node can be trusted for a given purpose. A node whose blocks are far fewer than its headers is still downloading and validating, and the field that tells whether it is in the initial block download says so directly. The book explains what its own printout shows: a blockchain height of 0 blocks and 83,999 headers, because the node first fetches the block headers from its peers to find the blockchain with the most proof of work and then goes on to download the full blocks, validating them as it goes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The numbers are a snapshot, and a node that is receiving blocks changes them every few minutes. A height equal to the headers does not by itself prove that the node is caught up with the network, since both come from the node's peers, and the verification progress is an estimate between zero and one, not a measure. The field that says that the node is in the initial block download is described by the source as debug information and as an estimate. An owner who needs certainty compares the best block hash with a block explorer or with a second node.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Network information (getnetworkinfo)

items.head: What it is
items.body: Network information is the answer to the call getnetworkinfo, one of the commands that the book lists beside the call for the chain, the mempool and the wallet when it says how to get information on the status of the node (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

rows: [n for n, b in names if 0xc09 & b]

items.body: The version number encodes three numbers: the source defines the client version as 10000 times the major number plus 100 times the minor number plus the build number, so release 31.1.0 is 310100 and the book's release 24.0.1 is 240001, and the user-agent string is built by writing the three numbers between the name Satoshi and slashes, following the specification in BIP 14 (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

slides.notes:
The answer tells the owner what the rest of the network sees. A node that offers fewer services than expected, or that has no connections, or that reports a network as not reachable, is not doing what its owner thinks. It also shows the settings that decide which transactions the node accepts, the minimum relay fee and the incremental fee, given in bitcoins per thousand virtual bytes, which is why the figure of 0.00001000 in the book's printout means one satoshi per virtual byte, and the figure of 0.000001 in the evidence means 0.1 satoshis per virtual byte, the value that the release notes of 30.0 give for the new default (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Service bits are unauthenticated advertisements, as the source itself says, so a peer that claims a service may not provide it, and the code must be robust against that (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The protocol version of the evidence, 70016, is not the constant in the newest source tree, which is 70017, because the tree is newer than the release, so two figures from different dates should not be compared as if they were errors. A last caution is the name of the user agent: it says Satoshi for historical reasons and is not a claim about who runs the node.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Wallet

items.head: What this section covers
items.body: The wallet group collects the concepts about the wallet that comes with Bitcoin Core. Chapter 1 introduced the wallet as the application with which a user holds and spends bitcoin, and the book says here that the reference implementation includes wallets next to the validation engine and the tools for block construction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In this software the wallet is optional: the build can leave it out, as the book's option to disable the reference wallet implementation shows, and a node can run without one (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
The three concepts follow the story of the format. The legacy wallet was the first kind, kept in a Berkeley DB file and described with keys alone.

slides.notes:
The wallet is where a node meets money. Everything else in the node concerns the shared record, whereas the wallet concerns the outputs that belong to its owner and the keys that spend them. Its storage format therefore matters to users more than most settings: a format that is retired makes old files unusable until they are converted. The concepts in this group give the current format, the retired one and the language of descriptions that the current one is built on.

Two cautions apply. The first is that this chapter gives only what the node needs in order to run; the book treats keys and wallets in its later chapters. The second is that the file of a wallet holds what is needed to spend the owner's funds, and Bitcoin Core's documentation points out that the file is not encrypted by default and that it must be backed up with the call provided for it, not by copying the file of a running node (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Concepts in this section: Descriptor wallet, Legacy wallet, Output descriptor, Output type.

slides.title: Descriptor wallet and Legacy wallet

items.head: Descriptor wallet
items.body: A descriptor wallet is a wallet whose content is a set of output descriptions, each stating one family of scripts that the wallet can receive to and spend from.

items.head: Legacy wallet
items.body: A legacy wallet is the kind of wallet that Bitcoin Core used before descriptors: a Berkeley DB database file holding the keys of the owner and the transactions that concern them.
The reason for the change lies in what a wallet must know.

slides.notes:
The descriptor wallet is the only kind that a current node can create. The release notes of 30.0 state that legacy wallets can no longer be created or loaded, and the run of release 31.1 in the evidence shows the consequence: asking for a wallet of the older kind fails with error code -4 and the message that the descriptors argument must be set to true because it is no longer possible to create a legacy wallet (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The change makes the wallet's behavior follow from descriptions that can be read, exported and checked, and no longer from a hidden list of keys.

The wallet file is not encrypted by default, and encrypting it needs a passphrase that cannot be recovered; the documentation warns that a lost passphrase loses the coins (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A copy or a backup should be taken with the backup call, not by copying a file that the running node is writing, and a wallet file must not be shared by two node instances (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Finally, a wallet made for the older format is not lost: it can be migrated to this one, as the concept of the legacy wallet explains.

---

The concept matters for two reasons. The first is historical: most of the books, articles and old backups that a learner will meet describe this wallet, with calls such as the ones for dumping or importing a private key. The second is practical: the release notes of 30.0 state that such wallets can no longer be created or loaded, and that they can be migrated to the descriptor format with the migratewallet call (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A user who owns an old file has to migrate it, because the node will not open it as it is.

A learner should not treat a command from an older text as current, because commands that the book's era used for the legacy wallet may no longer exist: the release notes name eleven of them as removed (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A migration is a change to something that holds money, so a backup should be made before it, and a migration is not reversible by the node. Hardware or software that still expects a legacy file must be updated as well.

slides.title: Output descriptor (1 of 4)

items.head: What it is
items.body: An output descriptor is a short piece of text in a simple language that describes a collection of output scripts.

items.cap: program OutputDescriptor, lines 1 to 11 of 40, run under Python 3.14.4

slides.notes:
Before descriptors, a wallet's backup contained keys and left the reader to guess which scripts they had been used for, and software of different makers could not agree on what a wallet contains. A descriptor states it completely, in a form that can be copied, printed and checked. The standard that defines the general syntax is BIP 380, and further BIPs define the individual expressions, which is why a descriptor written for one program can be read by another (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Wuille and Chow, 2021).

The checksum protects against accidents and not against attackers, since anybody can compute a valid one for any text, so it is no proof that a descriptor came from the person one thinks. Whether a checksum is required depends on the call: the BIP says it is optional for parsing and that applications may choose to reject descriptors without one, and Bitcoin Core requires it for only some calls, among them the one that derives addresses and the one that imports descriptors (Wuille and Chow, 2021) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).
