A descriptor that contains private keys is as secret as the keys, and one with only public keys reveals, to whoever reads it, every address of the wallet.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Output type
slides.sub: four descriptor kinds in the demo wallet

items.head: What it is
items.body: An output type is the form of the locking script of an output, which decides what the spender must show to spend it.

rows: sorted({re.match(r'[a-z]+', x['desc']).group(0) for x in d['descriptors']})

items.body: The descriptor of an output type is a function that takes a key, or several, and says how the locking script is built from it.

slides.notes:
The output type decides the address format and the cost of the payment. The older forms put all the data in the part of the transaction that counts fully towards its size, whereas the witness forms move the signature to the witness, which is discounted, as the weight concept explained. A descriptor wallet keeps one pair of descriptors for each type, one for receiving and one for change.

The abbreviations are easy to confuse. The lowercase function names of the descriptors, pkh, wpkh, sh and tr, and the uppercase names of the output types, P2PKH, P2WPKH, P2SH and P2TR, belong together but are not the same thing, and sh(wpkh) is one combined type and not two. The documentation's one-line descriptions are the reliable way to look up which is which.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Interface
slides.sub: The interface branch is about how other programs and people talk to a running node.
slides.notes:
The interface is what turns a node into a platform. Wallets, explorers, payment processors and research tools get their information about the chain from a node they trust, and they ask it through this interface, which is also the reason why the book lists "programmable access to the network and the blockchain" as one of the reasons for running a node of one's own (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The same interface can also spend funds, change settings and read private data when a wallet is loaded, so the way it is protected is as important as the way it is used.

The documentation of the project is blunt about the risk. The interface allows other programs to control Bitcoin Core, including spending funds from the wallets, affecting the verification of consensus rules, and reading private data; by default only a client on the same computer can reach it, and only with a valid credential, and the documentation says not to enable connections over the public Internet because the credentials are sent as clear text (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A reader who exposes the port to learn faster is taking the largest risk in the chapter.

slides.title: RPC interface

items.head: What this section covers
items.body: The RPC interface is the group of concepts that describe the programmatic doorway of Bitcoin Core. It gathers the idea of an application programming interface, the protocol that Bitcoin Core uses for it, the data format and the transport on which that protocol rides, and the two mechanisms with which the node checks the identity of a caller.
The concepts are taken from the outside inwards. The first is the interface in the general sense.

slides.notes:
Choosing an interface that rests on JSON and HTTP lets nearly every programming language use the node. The book remarks that any program that can make an HTTP request can call the interface, and that libraries in most popular programming languages wrap it so that the call looks like a function of the language (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The cost is that the node must decide whom to answer, and the group explains how it does so with a cookie that exists only while the node runs, or with credentials that are stored only in hashed form.

The first lines of the book's example are a call written for the command-line program curl, with the address 127.0.0.1, the default port 8332, a body that names the method, and a user name. The port is the node's own: the source gives 8332 for the main network, 18332 for the third test network, 48332 for the fourth and 38332 for the signet (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The log of the evidence node confirms that it bound to the address 127.0.0.1 and port 8332, after the attempt to bind the IPv6 address ::1 had failed (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Concepts in this section: Application programming interface, JSON-RPC interface, JSON data format, HTTP request, Cookie authentication, Hashed credentials (rpcauth), Salt, Keyed hash (HMAC).

slides.title: Application programming interface

items.head: What it is
items.body: An application programming interface, or API, is the defined way in which one program can use the functions of another. It names the requests that may be made, the information each request needs, and the form of the answer, and so it hides how the work is done behind a contract.

items.head: How it works
items.body: A method has a name and parameters, and it returns a result or an error.

slides.notes:
The API is the reason why one reference implementation can serve very different applications. A wallet, an exchange, a research script and a monitoring tool ask the same node different questions, and none of them needs to know how the node stores the blocks or checks the signatures. The book calls it programmable access to the network and the blockchain, and counts building applications that must validate transactions according to Bitcoin's consensus rules among the reasons for running one's own node (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

An interface is a promise only for as long as its owner keeps it. The documentation gives the grace period of one major version for deprecated features, and the chapter's own examples show a change: the field of warnings was a string and became an array of strings in release 28.0 (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A program that depends on the exact text of an answer, as opposed to its documented fields, breaks sooner. Finally, an API gives access, not trust: an answer from a node one does not control is only as good as that node.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: JSON-RPC interface

items.head: What it is
items.body: JSON-RPC is a protocol for remote procedure calls whose messages are written in JSON.

The two endpoints of the server are the root and a path for each wallet, and the documentation says that the second must be used for wallet requests when two or more wallets are loaded, as the helper does when it is given the name of a wallet (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

slides.notes:
The protocol keeps the interface small. A client needs to know only the name of a method and its parameters, and the answer tells the result or the error. Because the identifier comes back unchanged, a client can send many requests and still know which answer belongs to which. A request without an identifier is a notification, to which the server must not reply, a feature that Bitcoin Core supports for the newer version of the protocol (JSON-RPC Working Group, 2013) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The name remote procedure call hides a danger: the call looks like a local function and behaves like a network request, so it can fail, be slow, or be answered by something else. The documentation warns that other programs on the same machine can try to provide an interface on the same port to trick a user into revealing the credentials, and that the interface does not guarantee escaping of data beyond what JSON needs, so the data of an answer, for example a decoded string, must be handled as untrusted (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The older style is also still accepted, so a program written for it keeps working, which may hide differences in the error behavior.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: JSON data format

items.head: What it is
items.body: JSON, short for JavaScript Object Notation, is a text format for the serialization of structured data, which its standard describes as lightweight, text-based and independent of any language (Bray, 2017).

slides.notes:
The book calls JSON a very convenient way to present data that both humans and programs can easily read, and in the section on status information it says that the data is returned in JSON, a format that can easily be consumed by all programming languages while remaining quite human-readable (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This is why the same answer can be read by a person at the terminal and parsed by a program, and why the rest of the book can show results as pieces of text.

JSON is a data format, not a protocol, and by itself it says nothing about what a member means: the meaning of the member bits or of the member weight comes from the documentation of Bitcoin Core. The order of the members of an object has no meaning and should not be relied on. The format also has no comments and no way to say that a number is a hash or an amount, so a mistake in interpretation is not caught by the parser. The course returns to this point at the end of the chapter, where JSON is given a meaning by a context.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: HTTP request

items.head: What it is
items.body: The Hypertext Transfer Protocol, HTTP, is the protocol on which the web is built.

items.head: How it works
items.body: The POST method asks the target resource to process the representation enclosed in the request according to its own semantics, which is what a remote call needs, since the body names the method to run (Fielding et al., 2022).

slides.notes:
Using HTTP as the carrier means that a call can be made by any of the tools that already speak it, from a browser to a library of any language. The book shows curl, the versatile command-line HTTP client, and says that a program may use a generic HTTP library to build the call, as the example with curl does (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The manual of curl describes it as a tool for transferring data from or to a server using URLs, with options for the user, for the data to be sent without change, and for header fields (Stenberg, 2026).

Base64 is an encoding, not encryption, so anybody who can read the request can read the credentials, and plain HTTP offers no protection on its way; the documentation of the project says that the interface uses authentication but no encryption (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The status codes are also an indication of a different kind from the errors of the call: with the older protocol a failed call returns an HTTP error status, and with the newer one it returns 200 with an error member, unless the failure was in the HTTP server itself (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A program that checks only the HTTP status will misjudge one of them.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Cookie authentication

items.head: What it is
items.body: Cookie authentication is the default way in which Bitcoin Core decides who may call its interface.

The source creates 32 random bytes with the node's random-number generator, writes them as 64 hexadecimal digits after the fixed user name __cookie__ and a colon, and renames the finished file into place (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

slides.notes:
The method removes the need for the owner to invent and store a password. The init documentation says that a daemon run without any configuration uses a special cookie file for authentication, that the cookie is generated with random content when the daemon starts, and that read access to the file controls who can use the interface (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The project's security notes name this the preferred authentication method, because the secret is new at every start, never typed and never put into a configuration file (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Anyone who can read the cookie file controls the interface. The default file mode, owner only, is set by the process-wide file creation mask of 0077, and the documentation recommends that the data directory be readable only by the user and group of the node, with access to the interface controlled by group membership (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A cookie is also no solution for a client on another computer or a service that must survive restarts, because the secret changes each time; for these cases the stored credential of the next concept is used, as the book itself says by pointing to the helper script in the share folder (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Hashed credentials (rpcauth)

items.head: What it is
items.body: The rpcauth option is the way to give the interface a fixed credential without storing the password in plain text.

slides.notes:
A stored password in a configuration file is a secret on a disk that is copied, backed up and sometimes shared. Storing only a salted hash means that a leaked file does not reveal the password. The source of the node logs a warning when the older options for user and password are used, saying that they are less secure because the credentials are configured in plain text, and recommends cookie-based authentication or hashed credentials instead; the project's security notes name the script as the way to generate static credentials and the plain user and password options as the last fallback (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The hash protects the file, not the connection: the client still sends the password itself in each request, and the interface does not encrypt, so the credential is only as safe as the path between client and node (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A hashed credential also does not limit what the caller may do; the option rpcwhitelist can restrict the methods a user may call, but the documentation says that such restrictions should not be seen as robust security boundaries, and recommends system-level isolation instead (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A weak password remains weak, even though the hash is not reversible: it can be guessed offline by anyone who has the line.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Salt

items.head: What it is
items.body: A salt is a random value that is stored next to a hashed password and mixed into the hash.

The salt does not need to be secret, since it is stored in the open, but it must be random and different for each credential. The hash function used is the keyed hash of the next concept, with the salt in the place of the key.

slides.notes:
The server must be able to check a password without keeping it. It keeps the user, the salt and the hash, and when a request comes it computes the hash of the supplied password with the stored salt and compares. The salt means that two users with the same password have different stored values, and that an attacker cannot use one prepared table of hashes against all users. The line in the configuration file therefore reveals neither the password nor whether two accounts share one.

A salt protects the stored value and not the password in transit. The password is still sent with each request, and over plain HTTP it is readable by anybody who can see the traffic, as the Base64 concept explains. A salt also does not make a weak password strong; it only prevents the reuse of work across credentials. That is why the helper script offers to generate a long random password, 32 bytes in text form, instead of leaving the choice to the user.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Keyed hash (HMAC)

items.head: What it is
items.body: An HMAC, the keyed-hash message authentication code, is a hash function used with a key.

rows: v = hmac.new(b'Jefe', b'what do ya want for nothing?', hashlib.sha256).hexdigest().upper()

items.body: The sample code of the standard states the construction in a comment: SHA(K XOR opad, SHA(K XOR ipad, text)), two nested hashes in which the key, combined with two fixed padding bytes, is mixed in at each level (Eastlake and Hansen, 2011).

slides.notes:
A plain hash proves nothing about who made it, because anybody can compute it. A keyed hash can be produced only with the key, so it is evidence that the holder of the key made it. Bitcoin Core uses this in a modest way, as the way to turn a password and a salt into a stored value. The same construction appears in other parts of the system, where a secret key is needed to derive other keys.

An HMAC authenticates data; it does not encrypt it. The message can be read by anybody who sees it, and the HMAC proves only that the sender knew the key. In the rpcauth credential the key is the salt, which is not secret, so the HMAC is used here as a one-way function with a per-credential parameter and not as a proof of the sender's identity. A reader should keep the two uses apart.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Client

items.head: What this section covers
items.body: The client group collects the concepts about the programs that call the interface. A client is whatever makes a request to the node: a person at a terminal with the helper program, a script that builds the HTTP message itself, or an application that uses a library written for its language. The book goes through them in this order, starting with the help command of the helper, continuing with the curl command that the help prints, and ending with a Python library (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
The concepts are the command line, the helper program that runs on it, and the wrapper library.

slides.notes:
The choice of client decides how much of the protocol a user has to know. At the terminal one needs only the name of a method and its parameters. With a generic HTTP tool one must also write the body and manage the credential. With a wrapper library one writes a function call, and the library does the rest. The book remarks that the helper is very useful for exploring the API and testing functions, and that the whole point of an API is to access functions programmatically (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

All three clients are met in the chapter. The helper is used for the first calls, to list the commands, to get help on one of them and to ask for the hash of block 1000, which the book prints as 00000000c937983704a73af28acdec37b049d214adbda81d7e2a3dd146f6ed09 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The Python programs in the last part use the wrapper library, and in the evidence of this version the book's first program was run unchanged with the library at version 0.12.2 against the node of release 31.1 (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Concepts in this section: Command line, Command-line client (bitcoin-cli), Wrapper library.

slides.title: Command line

items.head: What it is
items.body: The command line is a way of using a computer by typing text commands in a terminal and reading the text that the programs print. A command is the name of a program followed by arguments, separated by spaces, and the program decides what to do with them.

The shell splits what is typed into words, the first being the program and the others its arguments, which the worked example shows with the standard library's splitting function for the command that asks for the hash of block 1000: three words, the program, the method and the height as text.

slides.notes:
The command line is the common ground of the people who run nodes: it works on a server without any graphical display, over a remote connection, and in scripts that can be repeated. It also leaves a record, because the text of a command can be copied into a document or a script, which is how the book can show an exact sequence of steps. The helper program of Bitcoin Core is made for it, as is the daemon with its options.

The command line is exact and unforgiving: a misplaced space or quote changes the meaning, and a command copied from a page may contain characters that look the same but are not, such as typographic quotation marks. Commands also run with the privileges of the user who types them, so a command copied from an unknown source can do harm, as the documentation says about configuration changes provided by others (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The history of the terminal may keep secrets typed as arguments, such as a password, which is a reason to use a prompt where one is offered.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Command-line client (bitcoin-cli)

items.head: What it is
items.body: The command-line client is the program bitcoin-cli, which the installed-files table of Bitcoin Core describes as the tool for making node and wallet RPC calls (Bitcoin Core, 2026).
The client reads the data directory to find the cookie, or the configured credential, and sends an HTTP request to the local port.

slides.notes:
The client lets a reader try the interface before writing any code. The book starts the section with the command help, which lists all RPC commands; adding the name of a command after help gives the description, the arguments, the result and two examples (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The first example in the book is bitcoin-cli getblockhash 1000, whose result, a block hash, shows that the node is running, accepting commands and holding the block, as the book puts it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The helper is a convenience and not a separate interface: everything it does is a call to the node, and a typing mistake becomes a request for the wrong thing. The positional form needs the parameters in the exact order, which for a method with many optional parameters is error-prone, and the named form is safer, as the documentation's example for creating a wallet shows (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book's printed results are from a node at a given height, and a reader's results will differ; the chapter itself warns that the examples assume the node is at least at block 775,072 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Wrapper library

items.head: What it is
items.body: A wrapper library is a package for a programming language that makes the node's interface look like ordinary functions of that language.

items.cap: program WrapperLibrary, lines 1 to 5 of 5, run under Python 3.14.4

slides.notes:
A wrapper takes away the work of building the request, finding the credentials, sending the message and decoding the answer, so that the programmer thinks in terms of the node's methods. The book contrasts it with the alternative of building the call with a generic HTTP library as shown with curl (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The price is a dependency: the wrapper must follow the changes of the node, and it is maintained by someone else. The documentation of python-bitcoinlib says that its interface should work with Bitcoin Core 24.0 or later, and the evidence of this version confirms that the book's first program runs with version 0.12.2 on Python 3.14.4 against the release 31.1 (Todd, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

A wrapper hides the protocol and so can hide failures: it raises an error of its own when the node reports one, it needs the node to be running and reachable, and it needs a credential that works, which is the usual cause of failure. A library that is not maintained may lack the newest methods or the newest fields. The version in the book's era, 0.12.2, dates from June 2023, a point the research record of this chapter checks against the package index. And a wrapper is only a client of the node: the quality of the answers is the quality of the node behind it.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Data
slides.sub: The data branch is about what a node holds and what the interface shows of it: the transactions that move value, the blocks that gather them into the shared record, and the state of the chain that results.
slides.notes:
A student who understands the fields can check the node's answers, which is the point of running a node. The book says that a transaction ID is not authoritative before confirmation, that a block's confirmations tell its depth, and that the median time of the block is a time measurement harder for miners to manipulate (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Each of these statements is a claim about how the system is built, and each can be tested on data that anybody can fetch. The branch therefore pairs each field with a computation that reproduces it from the raw bytes.

Two cautions apply to the whole branch. The first is that the data in the book belong to a moment: the confirmations of a block grow with every new block, and the block of the later example is so old that its figures are history only. The second is that the book contains one printed result that does not match its script. The program that adds the outputs of block 775072 prints 10,322.07722534 BTC and explains it as including a reward of 25 BTC, but the reward at that height is 6.25 BTC, and the sum of all outputs of that block is 5,863.00566521 BTC, as the executed checks of this chapter show (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

slides.title: Transaction

items.head: What this section covers
items.body: The transaction group collects the concepts about the objects that carry value. Chapter 2 introduced the transaction with its inputs, outputs and fee; this group looks at the same object as a node sees it, first as a string of bytes, then as a decoded structure with fields, with an identifier and with a cost in block space.
The concepts follow the path from bytes to meaning.

slides.notes:
How a transaction is stored decides how it is identified and how much it costs. A change in the serialization introduced the witness, a part of the transaction that is not included in the old identifier, and with it a second identifier and a new measure of size. A reader who knows only the simple picture of inputs and outputs will not be able to explain why Alice's transaction has a size of 194 bytes and a virtual size of 143, or why it has two identifiers. This group explains why.

The group's concepts are met in the output of the two commands of the book: the first returns the serialized transaction in hexadecimal notation, and the second decodes it into the fields shown in the chapter (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). They are met again in every block explorer and every wallet, which show the same fields under other names. The evidence of this version decodes the book's hexadecimal with both the real release 31.1 and a short Python program, and the two agree on every field (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Concepts in this section: Transaction serialization, Decoded transaction, Segregated witness, Transaction weight, Transaction identifier (txid and wtxid), Transaction malleability.

slides.title: Transaction serialization (1 of 5)
slides.sub: the hexadecimal string of Alice's transaction

items.head: What it is
items.body: Serialization is the writing of a structured object as a sequence of bytes, so that it can be stored or sent.

items.cap: program TransactionSerialization, lines 1 to 10 of 48, run under Python 3.14.4

slides.notes:
A precise byte layout is what lets independent programs agree. The specification BIP 144 defines the layout with witness data: a four-byte version, a marker byte that must be zero, a flag byte that must be nonzero, the number of inputs, the inputs, the number of outputs, the outputs, the witnesses and a four-byte lock time (Lombrozo and Wuille, 2016). The marker is zero so that the layout is never mistaken for a valid transaction by a program that does not know about witnesses, because in the old layout a zero would mean a transaction with no inputs (Lombrozo and Wuille, 2016).

The layout has a short and a long form. A transaction with no witness is written without the marker and the flag, and that is the form that is hashed to get the old identifier, so one transaction has two serializations. A parser that assumes one of them will misread the other, which is the reason why the call that decodes a raw transaction has an option to tell whether the hexadecimal is in the witness form, and uses a heuristic when it is not told (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The numbers are also written the unexpected way round: byte order in identifiers is reversed between the display and the bytes that are hashed.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
