slides.title: Decoded transaction

items.head: What it is
items.body: A decoded transaction is the structure that results from reading the bytes of a serialized transaction and naming each field. The command decoderawtransaction takes the hexadecimal string and returns a JSON object (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The decoding code reads the bytes as the serialization concept describes and converts what it reads: the satoshi values become amounts in bitcoin by dividing by 100,000,000, the scripts are shown as assembly and as hexadecimal, the type of each script is recognized from its pattern, and for a known type an address is derived and shown.

slides.notes:
Decoding turns an opaque string into something a person can check. The book remarks that the decode shows all the components of the transaction, and that following the identifier of the input to the previous transaction lets a reader walk back through the chain of transactions as the coins pass from one owner to the next (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Anyone who distrusts a wallet or an explorer can run the same decoding on their own node, which is the independent check that the chapter advocates.

The decoder shows what the bytes say, not whether they are valid or confirmed. A transaction may be well formed and still spend an output that does not exist, or one that is already spent. The values are given as decimal fractions of a bitcoin, with eight decimals, which a floating-point program should not use for money arithmetic. And the book's example gives the address of an output only because the node was able to derive it from the script: an output whose script has no standard form has no address. The call that fetches a transaction by identifier only works for mempool transactions unless the transaction index is on, or the block is named (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Segregated witness and Transaction weight

items.head: Segregated witness
items.body: Segregated witness, often written SegWit, is an upgrade that separates the data that prove a spending right, the signatures, from the rest of the transaction.
Software that knows the upgrade finds a witness program in an output script: a version number followed by a short piece of data.

items.head: Transaction weight
items.body: The weight of a transaction is a measure of the block space it uses, in weight units.
Weight units make the witness discount a precise rule.

slides.notes:
The upgrade solved two problems. It removed the witness from the data that the transaction identifier covers, so that a third party can no longer change an identifier by changing a signature, a point that the malleability concept develops. And it changed the way block space is measured: BIP 141 defines the weight of a block as the base size times three plus the total size, and limits it to 4,000,000, so witness bytes count one unit each while all the other bytes count four (Lombrozo et al., 2015). Witness data are therefore cheaper than other data.

The upgrade was designed to be a soft fork: old nodes see an output script with a version and a program and consider anyone able to spend it, while upgraded nodes enforce the new rules, so old nodes keep accepting the chain without understanding the witness (Lombrozo et al., 2015). This also means that a node which does not understand witnesses cannot verify the signatures of such transactions, even though it accepts them, which is a reason to run current software. The upgrade was activated at height 481824 on the main network, a constant that Bitcoin Core's chain parameters record (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

---

Weight is the unit in which the limit of a block is set. The source of the consensus rules gives the maximum block weight as 4,000,000 and the witness scale factor as 4, so a block of only old-style bytes can contain 1,000,000 of them, and a block with witnesses can contain more (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Weight is also the basis of the fee rate that chapter 2 introduced: a fee rate in satoshis per virtual byte divides the fee by the weight over four, which is why the decoded answer shows both the size and the virtual size.

Virtual bytes are not bytes, and the discount does not reduce the data that nodes must store or send: a node still downloads and stores all 194 bytes. The limit on weight is a consensus rule, whereas the policy of which transactions a node relays has other limits, one of which is the minimum fee rate, so a transaction of valid weight may still not be relayed. A last point is that older material speaks of a block limit of one megabyte, a rule that the upgrade replaced by the limit of weight, and the figure quoted in the book for the block of the later example, 4179 bytes, is far below either.

slides.title: Transaction identifier (txid and wtxid)

items.head: What it is
items.body: A transaction identifier is the name of a transaction: the double SHA-256 hash of its serialization, written with the bytes in reverse order. The transaction has two of them.

items.cap: program TransactionIdentifier, lines 48 to 48 of 48, run under Python 3.14.4

items.body: Lines 1 to 47 are the parser already on the slides; only what follows differs.

slides.notes:
Identifiers are how everything refers to a transaction: the inputs of later transactions, the lists in blocks, the Merkle tree, the requests to the node. Having a second identifier that covers the witness allows the network to commit to the signatures in the block without changing what the old identifier covers. If no input uses a witness, the two identifiers are equal (Lombrozo et al., 2015). The book's tip adds the warning that a txid is not authoritative, a point that the malleability concept develops (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A txid can be looked up in the block files only with the transaction index or with the name of the block, as the earlier concepts explain, and the book warns that the absence of a txid from the blockchain does not mean the transaction was not processed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The wtxid is the more specific name, and is the one used when transactions are announced to peers in current protocols. It is also not secret, and not an address: two parties who know the identifier know only which transaction is meant.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Transaction malleability
slides.sub: changing a signature changes the wtxid but not the txid

items.head: What it is
items.body: Transaction malleability is the possibility that a transaction can be changed by a third party before it is confirmed, so that its identifier changes while what it does stays the same.

lines: result = (d(ws)[::-1].hex() == wtxid, d(raw[:4] + raw[6:out_end] + ws[wit_end:])[::-1].hex() == txid)
items.cap: program TransactionMalleability, lines 48 to 51 of 51, run under Python 3.14.4

items.body: Lines 1 to 47 are the parser already on the slides; only what follows differs.

slides.notes:
A program that watches for a payment by its txid can be misled. If a transaction is changed in transit and the changed version is the one that is confirmed, the original identifier never appears in a block, and a program that waits for it would conclude that the payment failed although the money moved. The book's advice is to treat the txid as authoritative only after confirmation: after the transaction is included in a block, its txid cannot change unless a reorganization removes that block from the best chain, and reorganizations are rare after several confirmations (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Segregated witness does not make every transaction immune. A transaction that spends an old-style output still has its signature script in the txid, and a transaction can still be replaced by a conflicting one that spends the same inputs, which is a different matter from malleability, since it has different outputs or a different meaning. The wtxid, in turn, can still change with the witness. And the TIP of the book is still true for the careful programmer: use the transaction's confirmation, not only its identifier, to know that a payment was made.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Block

items.head: What this section covers
items.body: The block group collects the concepts about the unit in which transactions are recorded. A block holds a header, which is a small fixed-size summary, and a list of transactions, which makes up most of its size; the book of the chapter on the blockchain says that the header is 80 bytes while the transactions of a block can total much more (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
The concepts of the group go from the outside to the inside.

slides.notes:
Knowing the block's fields is knowing how the chain is held together. Each block names its parent by the hash of its header, so changing anything in a block changes its hash and breaks the link to the next. The header also commits to the transactions through the Merkle root, to the work that was spent through the target and the nonce, and to the time through the timestamp. The book says of the fields of the answer that some are used for security and proof of work: merkle root, nonce, bits, difficulty and chainwork (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The reader meets the group in the answer of the block command for block 123456 in the book: its hash, 13 transactions, a height, the number of confirmations, the version, the Merkle root, the time, the median time, the nonce, the bits, the difficulty, the chain work, the sizes and the list of transaction identifiers (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The evidence of this version confirms the hash of this block from its header, its Merkle root from its 13 identifiers, and its difficulty from its bits, using the public data of an explorer (Blockstream, 2026).

Concepts in this section: Block height, Block hash, Block header, Block weight, Merkle root, Block subsidy, Compact target (bits), Difficulty, Median time past.

slides.title: Block height

items.head: What it is
items.body: The height of a block is its position in the chain: the number of blocks that precede it. The book says that the height tells how many blocks preceded the block, and the glossary of the chapter on the blockchain adds that the first block, the genesis block, is at height 0 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
The height is not stored in the header and is not part of a block's identity: it is the length of the path to the genesis block, and the node counts it in its index.

slides.notes:
Heights give people a convenient name for a block, because they are short and ordered. A hash identifies a block without doubt, but it cannot be read or ordered; a height can be said aloud and compared. The book says that blocks can be referenced either by their height or by their hash, and the first command of the exploration, getblockhash, takes a height and returns the block header hash (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The consensus rules also use heights: they decide when the reward is halved and when an upgrade becomes active.

Height 0 is the first block and not the second, so the number of blocks in a chain is its height plus one. A height is also not a proof: the same height names different blocks on different chains, and BIP 34 made the height a part of the coinbase of each block precisely so that it is unambiguous (Andresen, 2012). The height of the tip changes every ten minutes or so, and any figure quoted in the book, such as the assumption that the node is at least at block 775,072, is a snapshot of that day (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Block hash

items.head: What it is
items.body: The block hash is the identifier of a block.

rows: h = struct.pack('<I', b['version']) + bytes.fromhex(b['previousblockhash'])[::-1] + bytes.fromhex(b['merkle_root'])[::-1] + struct.pack('<III', b['timestamp'], b['bits'], b['nonce'])

items.body: The header's fields are packed in a fixed order into 80 bytes: the version as four bytes with the least significant first, the 32 bytes of the previous block hash and 32 bytes of the Merkle root, both reversed from their display order, and the time, the bits and the nonce as four bytes each. The packed bytes are put through SHA-256 twice, and the 32-byte result is reversed to produce the familiar display.

slides.notes:
A single hash stands for the entire block, because the header contains the Merkle root of the transactions, and the next block's header contains this hash as the previous block hash. Anyone who knows the hash of the latest block can in principle check the whole chain behind it. The book says that the hash identifies a block uniquely and unambiguously and can be independently derived by any node by hashing the header (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A hash is not an authority. It tells which block is meant, not whether the block is valid or part of the best chain; a block with a very small hash can still be invalid because of a transaction in it. The display order differs from the order used in computation, and a program that forgets to reverse the bytes gets a different value. And the explorer's data used here are a secondary source: the check confirms that the explorer's fields are consistent with each other, which is what the hash promises, not that the explorer is honest about the chain.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Block header and Block weight

items.head: Block header
items.body: The block header is the summary at the head of every block.
Each field has a role in the chain. The previous block hash links the block to its parent. The Merkle root ties the transactions to the header.

items.head: Block weight
items.body: The weight of a block is its size in weight units, calculated like the weight of a transaction: BIP 141 defines it as the base size times three plus the total size, where the base size is the size without witness data and the total size is the size with it (Lombrozo et al., 2015).

slides.notes:
The header is small on purpose. Because it commits to everything else, a program that holds only the headers can follow the chain and its work without the transactions. This is what the node in the book does when it starts: it first fetches the block headers from its peers to find the blockchain with the most proof of work, and afterward continues to download the full blocks (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Nakamoto's paper made the same point about lighter programs: a user needs to keep only a copy of the block headers of the longest proof-of-work chain (Nakamoto, 2008).

The version field no longer means a version. The book's table says it was originally a version field and its use has evolved; the upgrade mechanism of BIP 9 uses its bits to signal readiness, as the soft fork concept explains (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille et al., 2015). The header's time is set by the miner and is only roughly right. And the header does not contain the number of transactions, the block's height or its hash, which are all derived.

---

The limit decides how many transactions a block can hold, and so how much the network can do in ten minutes. It replaced the earlier limit of 1,000,000 bytes of total size with a combined measure, so that witness data, which is cheaper to verify and does not burden the set of unspent outputs, is charged less (Lombrozo et al., 2015). The limit is also a constant in the source: the maximum block weight is 4,000,000, and the witness scale factor is 4 (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Weight is not the same as size and the two should not be mixed. A tool that reports a block size in bytes and one that reports it in virtual bytes give different numbers for the same block, and a reader who compares them with the limit of 4,000,000 must use the weight. The limit is also a rule for miners, not for relay nodes, which means that a block over the limit is invalid, whereas a transaction is only rejected by policy before that.

slides.title: Merkle root
slides.sub: the Merkle root of the block's transactions

items.head: What it is
items.body: The Merkle root is the single hash in a block header that stands for all the transactions of the block.

lines: level = [d(level[i] + level[i + 1]) for i in range(0, len(level), 2)]
items.cap: program MerkleRoot, lines 1 to 7 of 7, run under Python 3.14.4

slides.notes:
The root makes the header a commitment to the contents. Changing, adding, removing or reordering any transaction changes the root, which changes the header and so the block hash, and the proof of work would have to be redone. It also allows a short proof of membership: to show that one transaction is in a block, one needs only the hashes along the path from the transaction to the root, not the whole block, a property that Nakamoto's paper describes when it explains how payments can be verified without running a full node (Nakamoto, 2008).

The rule of duplicating the last element has a known weakness: two different lists of transactions can give the same root if the later one repeats the last transaction, and for this reason a node must check a block's transactions for duplication in addition to the root. The root is also computed from txids, not wtxids, so it does not commit to the witnesses; the second tree of BIP 141 does (Lombrozo et al., 2015). And a root is not evidence of validity: it proves only that the listed transactions are those that the miner hashed.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Block subsidy

items.head: What it is
items.body: The block subsidy is the amount of new bitcoin that a block creates, which the miner may claim in the first transaction of the block, the coinbase transaction.

items.head: How it works
items.body: The coinbase transaction cannot create more than the subsidy plus the fees of the block, and the amount is checked by every node.

slides.notes:
The schedule is what makes the supply of bitcoin finite and predictable. The amounts are counted in satoshis, 100,000,000 to a bitcoin, so each shift right halves an integer; the sum of all the subsidies over the 64 possible periods is 2,099,999,997,690,000 satoshis, which is slightly below 21 million bitcoins by 2,310,000 satoshis, because of the rounding in the shifts, as the worked checks of this branch compute (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The consensus constant for the maximum amount of money is 21,000,000 times the number of satoshis in a bitcoin (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The book's text mentions a reward of 25 BTC and 0.0909 BTC in fees for the block of its example, and the total of 10,322.07722534 BTC. Neither matches block 775072: its reward is 6.25 BTC, its fees are 0.08799108 BTC, and the sum of all its outputs is 5,863.00566521 BTC, so the printed result does not belong to that block, and a student who compares with an explorer, as the book suggests, will find the difference (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Blockstream, 2026). 25 BTC was the reward for blocks 420,000 to 629,999. The error shows why printed numbers should be checked.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Compact target (bits)

items.head: What it is
items.body: The compact target is the way in which the header records the proof-of-work target in only four bytes. The target is a 256-bit number that the hash of a valid block must not exceed, as chapter 2 explained for the difficulty target, and a 256-bit number would need 32 bytes.

The source decodes the field with two lines: the size is the value shifted right by 24 bits, the word is the value masked by 0x007fffff, and the target is the word shifted left by 8 times the size minus 3 bits, that is, by size minus three bytes (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

slides.notes:
Four bytes were enough because the target needs only a few digits of precision: it changes in small steps, and the lower digits would not matter. A compact form keeps the header at 80 bytes. The chain information of the current release shows both the compact form, in the field bits, and the target in full, which the book's printout of 2023 does not have (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The form also has a sign bit, a legacy of the number type it was borrowed from, which Bitcoin Core rejects as a target when it is set.

Because only three bytes of the target are kept, the true target that the hash is compared with is the decoded one, not the one the retargeting formula first computed, and a table of difficulties from a program that uses the full-precision number can differ by a tiny amount from one that uses bits. A second caution is the sign bit: the code reduces the mantissa and raises the size if the top bit of the three bytes is set, so values such as 0x1d00ffff and not 0x1d0100.. are seen in practice. And the header's field is named bits in the answer but target in the book's table (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Difficulty

items.head: What it is
items.body: The difficulty is a number that tells how much harder it is to produce a valid block than it was at the start. The glossary of the book defines it as a network-wide setting that controls how much computation is required to produce a proof of work (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The program in Bitcoin Core computes it from the bits with floating-point arithmetic: it takes 0x0000ffff divided by the mantissa, and multiplies or divides by 256 until the exponent is 29, the value for the easiest target (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

slides.notes:
The network keeps the time between blocks near ten minutes by changing the difficulty. The consensus parameters give a target spacing of 10 minutes and a target timespan of two weeks, which is 2016 blocks; after every 2016 blocks the target is multiplied by the time the last 2016 blocks actually took and divided by two weeks, and the change in one step is limited to a factor of four in either direction (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book says that every node retargets independently, every 2,016 blocks, and notes a small bias of 0.05 percent toward higher difficulty because the calculation uses 2,015 intervals (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Difficulty is a result and not a setting that anyone chooses: it follows the hash rate of miners with a delay of up to two weeks, so a sudden fall in mining power slows blocks until the next adjustment. It is also relative: a difficulty of 157,416 at one time and one of 53,911,173,001,054 at another, the figure printed in the book's cookie example, say how the work grew, not how much work either was (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A change in a test network may follow different rules, since the parameters allow a minimum-difficulty exception there (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Median time past

items.head: What it is
items.body: The median time past, often written MTP, is a clock that the chain defines for itself. For a block it is the median, the middle value in sorted order, of the timestamps of that block and the ten before it. Bitcoin Core's source states the number of blocks as the constant 11, sorts the times and returns the element in the middle (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The worked example takes the times of blocks 123446 to 123456, the eleven blocks ending with block 123456, sorts them and picks the sixth, which is 1305197900, the time of block 123451. This is exactly the value the node reports.

slides.notes:
The timestamps in headers are set by the miners, who have some latitude, and the book explains the danger: a miner could set the time in the future to lower the difficulty, or in the past to make it look as if blocks were slow, or to collect the fees of transactions with time locks that have not matured (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The median of eleven blocks is hard for one miner to move; BIP 113 made it the time that the checks on time locks use, so that the incentive to lie disappears (Kerin and Friedenbach, 2015).

The book describes the field as the median time of the 11 blocks that precede the block, but the code includes the block itself. The eleven blocks that precede block 123456 are blocks 123445 to 123455, whose median is 1305195947, not the 1305197900 that the node prints, so the sentence of the chapter is slightly off, and the median of the chapter on mining is the one that the field shows (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Timestamps are also not required to increase from block to block, only to exceed the median, so a sorted list of times can differ from the order of blocks.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Chain state

items.head: What this section covers
items.body: The chain state group collects the concepts that describe the blocks as a whole: which chain is the true one, how much work it represents, how deep a block is in it, and what happens when the node changes its mind. The word has a second meaning in Bitcoin Core, where the chain state is also the name of the database of unspent outputs, as the earlier concept on the set of unspent outputs explained; here the word means the shape of the chain (Bitcoin Core, 2026).
The order is from the rule to its consequences.

slides.notes:
A blockchain is not a single list but a tree, since two miners may find blocks at about the same time. The rule that resolves the tree is simple, and everything a user can trust depends on it. The book says that by selecting the greatest-cumulative-work valid chain all nodes eventually achieve network-wide consensus, and that temporary discrepancies between chains are resolved as more work is added (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The concepts of this group make that rule precise.

The group shows in the answers of the node: the chain work in the chain information and in the block data, the confirmations in the block data and the transaction data, and the reorganization only when the best chain changes, an event that the log records. The book's tip about transaction IDs refers to it, since a txid can change only if a reorganization removes the block that holds the transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Concepts in this section: Best chain, Chain work, Confirmation, Chain reorganization, Fork.

slides.title: Best chain
slides.sub: the chain with the most work

items.head: What it is
items.body: The best chain is the chain of valid blocks that a node regards as the true record.

rows: (a_work < b_work, max([('A', a_work), ('B', b_work)], key=lambda c: c[1])[0])

items.head: How it works
items.body: Work, not length, decides. The chain work concept shows how to measure it: a block with a smaller target represents more expected hashes.

slides.notes:
Without such a rule nodes would not agree, and without agreement there would be no single record of who owns what. Because blocks are found by a random process, two miners sometimes find a block at nearly the same time, and the chain forks: the glossary of the book describes this accidental fork as the situation when two or more blocks have the same height (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The rule tells every node which branch to follow, and as the next block is found on one of them, that branch gains work and the other is abandoned.

The best chain is a local judgment that nodes make with the same rule, not an announcement. At any moment two honest nodes can briefly hold different tips, and a payment in a block at the tip is not final. The longest-chain wording of the paper is a shorthand that was precise in a time when every block had the same difficulty, and the more exact wording is the one with the most work. Also, the rule applies only to valid blocks, and a chain with more work that contains an invalid block is not the best chain.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Chain work and Confirmation

items.head: Chain work
items.body: The chain work is the total amount of proof of work behind a block, expressed as the expected number of hashes needed to produce the chain up to it.

items.head: Confirmation
items.body: A confirmation is a block added at or above the block that contains a transaction.
Each new block extends the chain that already contains the transaction, so the number grows by one with every block on the best chain.

slides.notes:
This is the quantity that nodes compare to choose the best chain. The source of Bitcoin Core stores it in the index entry of each block, described as the total amount of work, the expected number of hashes, in the chain up to and including that block (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Because it adds numbers that depend only on the targets in the headers, it is the same in every node, and a node can compute the work of a chain from its headers alone, before having any transactions, which is why the node of the book fetches headers first (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The chain work counts expected work and not work actually done: the miner of a block may have been lucky or unlucky. It is also not a measure of the value of the chain, only of its cost to reproduce. The number is large and is shown in hexadecimal with leading zeros, which makes it easy to misread; a comparison of two such strings is a comparison of numbers with the same number of digits. And it is a quantity that the node computes itself from the headers, so it is not something that a peer tells it.

---

Confirmations are how a user decides when a payment is safe enough. A transaction in the mempool has none and can be replaced or dropped; one in a block at the tip has one and can still be undone by a reorganization; with each block on top, undoing it needs more work. The glossary says that six or more confirmations is considered sufficient proof that a transaction cannot be reversed, and the book's tip says that reorganizations are rare after a transaction has several confirmations (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). How many are enough depends on the value.

A confirmation is a count, not a guarantee; its meaning grows with the work of the blocks, and a confirmation in a low-difficulty chain is worth less. The conventional six is a convention of the book and of its era, not a rule of the protocol, and a large payment may warrant waiting for more. Another trap is that different programs count differently: some start from zero for a transaction in the tip block, while Bitcoin Core counts that block as the first confirmation (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

slides.title: Chain reorganization
slides.sub: switching to a branch with more work

items.head: What it is
items.body: A reorganization is the event in which a node changes which chain it regards as the best.

When the new chain has more work, the node disconnects the blocks of the old branch from the tip down to the point where the branches split, which restores the outputs those blocks spent and removes the ones they created in the set of unspent outputs, and then connects the blocks of the new branch. The transactions of the disconnected blocks that are not in the new blocks go back to the mempool, where they may be mined again.

slides.notes:
Reorganizations are the mechanism by which the network resolves forks without any authority. They matter to a user because they are the only way in which a confirmed transaction can become unconfirmed. The book's tip says the txid of a confirmed transaction cannot change unless there is a reorganization that removes the block from the best chain, and that such reorganizations are rare after a transaction has several confirmations (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Most reorganizations are only one block deep.

A reorganization does not undo a payment by itself: the transaction usually returns to the pool and is confirmed again in a later block, unless it conflicts with a transaction in the new chain, for instance one that spent the same output. The dangerous case is a double spend, in which the sender pays twice and tries to make the second payment win, and this is the attack that the number of confirmations guards against. A last caution is the scale: after an attack, a deeper reorganization needs more work than the honest network, and the argument depends on no single party controlling most of it (Nakamoto, 2008).

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Fork

items.head: What it is
items.body: A fork is a point where the chain of blocks divides into two branches.

rows: tips = sorted(b for b in blocks if not any(p == b for p, h in blocks.values()))
(tips, max(tips, key=lambda b: blocks[b][1]), sorted(b for b, (p, h) in blocks.items() if h == 1))

items.body: At a fork each node has seen the blocks in a different order and may have a different tip until one branch is extended. The node stores both branches in its block index and tracks the work of each, and when a branch overtakes the other it switches, as the concept of reorganization explains.

slides.notes:
Forks are how a distributed network without a central clock behaves, and they are resolved by the rule that a node follows the branch with the most proof of work. The shorter branch is abandoned, its blocks become stale, and the transactions in them return to the pool, which is what a reorganization does. Understanding the accidental fork is what makes the advice about waiting for confirmations sensible, since the block that ends a payment's journey is safe only when a branch has grown on top of it.

Not every split is a fork of the chain. Two nodes can disagree for a moment about the tip because a block has not reached one of them yet, and this is normal, not a fork. And a software fork, in which somebody copies the code and changes it, creates a new program but not a new chain unless its rules are incompatible with the old ones and someone runs it on the same network.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Ecosystem
slides.sub: The ecosystem branch is about the software around the reference implementation and about how a person can trust what they download.
slides.notes:
A node is only as trustworthy as the software it runs, because the node is the thing that checks the rules on the owner's behalf. If the program has been altered on its way to the computer, every answer it gives is worthless, however carefully the owner reads the output. The branch therefore treats the download as the first link of the chain of verification, before the first block is validated, and treats the choice of a library as a decision that can be examined with data rather than with taste.

The evidence for this branch comes from the real release 31.1 of Bitcoin Core: the file of checksums that the project publishes next to its programs, the file of signatures on it, and the documentation of the project's own tools for checking them (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The second kind of evidence is the data of the package registries on the toolkits that the book lists, which were queried on the day this chapter was prepared (Package registries, 2026). Both are saved in the repository of the course, so that the statements of the branch can be recomputed instead of believed.

slides.title: Assurance

items.head: What this section covers
items.body: Assurance is the group of concepts that answer the question how do I know. In this chapter it covers the evidence one can gather about a program before trusting it, namely the checksum published for the download, the signatures on that checksum and the build that makes the files reproducible, and the evidence one can gather about a library before depending on it, namely its latest release in a package registry. The common feature is that each statement can be checked by a computation on saved files and does not depend on the reputation of whoever makes it.

slides.notes:
The distinction between checking and trusting is the course's theme in miniature. The documentation of the build tooling of Bitcoin Core puts it as the wish to audit and reproduce the toolchain instead of blindly trusting binary downloads (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A reader who has taken this chapter's own advice and runs a node has made the same choice for the data: instead of trusting a block explorer, the reader verifies the chain. Assurance extends the choice to the software that does the verifying, and it also shows where the choice ends, since some trust always remains and the useful question is which trust is left.

None of the results of this group is a proof of safety. A matching checksum shows that two files are the same, not that either is harmless, and a good signature shows that a key signed, not who holds the key. A recent release in a registry shows activity, not quality. The concepts below state the limit of each check next to the check.

Concepts in this section: Release verification, Checksum, OpenPGP signature, Reproducible build, Package registry, Alternative toolkit.

slides.title: Release verification

items.head: What it is
items.body: Release verification is the check of a downloaded program against what the project published, done before the program is run.

The project ships a script for the whole procedure, which first checks whether the file of checksums is valid based upon a plurality of signatures and then downloads the files named in it and checks that their hashes are as expected (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

slides.notes:
A downloaded program runs with the rights of the person who starts it, so a file that was altered on the way is the most direct way to compromise a node. The documentation of the project explains that, as of version 22.0, releases are signed by a number of public keys on the basis of the signature repository, that the end user decides which of these keys to trust, and that the downloaded programs are then hashed and compared to the signed list of checksums (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The user, and not the web site that hosts the file, is the party who decides whom to believe, which is why the check protects against a web site or a mirror that has been tampered with.

The check has a limit that the saved evidence states itself: the keys used for the 11 good signatures came from the signature repository of the project and not from an independent source, so the result shows consistency and does not establish trust in the keys. A careful user obtains the keys of people they have reason to trust by a different path from the one that delivered the file, and then insists on a threshold. A matching checksum alone, from the same web page as the file, would prove only that the page is consistent with itself. The check also says nothing about whether the software has bugs, only that it is the software the builders produced.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Checksum

items.head: What it is
items.body: A checksum is a short value computed from the whole content of a file, which can be compared with a value computed elsewhere to decide whether the two files are the same. The checksums used for Bitcoin Core's releases are the SHA-256 hash function that chapter 2 explained, applied to the bytes of the file.

items.head: How it works
items.body: The way a checksum behaves is best seen on a small change.

slides.notes:
A checksum makes comparison cheap. Two files of ninety million bytes cannot be compared by looking at them, and sending one to a person who holds the other would be as costly as downloading it again, but their two digests of 64 characters can be compared in a moment, in a message or on a page. The same standard states the property that makes this useful: any change to a message in transit will, with very high probability, result in a different message digest (Eastlake and Hansen, 2011). A flipped bit in a bad download is therefore detected as surely as a deliberate change.

A checksum detects change; it does not say who made the file. If an attacker can replace the file, the attacker can replace the line of checksums that sits on the same server, and the check will pass. That is why the project signs the list of checksums, and why the signature, not the checksum, is what ties the list to people. The second thing to watch is the comparison: a checksum is compared as text, and a copy that changed a letter or lost a character will fail, while a glance at the first few characters is not a check at all, since the standard's guarantee holds for the whole value.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: OpenPGP signature

items.head: What it is
items.body: OpenPGP is a standard for the message formats used in secure messages and signed files. Its specification says that OpenPGP provides encryption with public key or symmetric cryptographic algorithms, digital signatures, compression and key management (Wouters et al., 2024).
The saved run counted, for the signatures on the list, the checks that reported a good signature, and the count was 11.

slides.notes:
The signature gives the checksum list an author. Without it the list is an assertion by whoever controls the web server, and with it the list is an assertion by a key, which the user can decide to trust or not. Several signatures on the same list add something more: a list that is signed by several independent builders is accepted only if each of them produced the same files, so that an attacker would have to compromise many of them. The documentation of the project describes this as a check based upon a plurality of signatures (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

A good signature from a key that was imported from the same place as the file proves little about authenticity, and the saved check of this chapter states this limit in its own output. Keys also expire or are revoked, and the specification of the format has fields and packets for both, so a signature by a revoked key should not be counted (Wouters et al., 2024). The third thing to watch is the difference between this signature and the one in a bitcoin transaction: both use public-key cryptography and both are called signatures, but the OpenPGP one follows a general file format, whereas the transaction signature is a part of the rules of the network and is checked by every node.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Reproducible build

items.head: What it is
items.body: A reproducible build is a way of compiling a program such that everybody who follows the same steps on the same source gets exactly the same files, byte for byte.

rows: ('bitcoin-31.1.tar.gz' in sums, [n for n in sums if n.endswith('x86_64-linux-gnu.tar.gz')])

items.body: The reproducibility rests on removing every source of difference between builds.

slides.notes:
Reproducibility turns a download into something that can be verified from the source. If the release files could depend on the builder's machine, nobody could say whether a file differed from the source because of the machine or because of an attack. If they cannot, then a builder who rebuilds the release and obtains the same checksums as the project has confirmed that the published files correspond to the published source, and the more builders do it, the harder it is for any single one of them to be tricked or bribed.

Reproducibility is evidence about the build and not about the source: the builders confirm that the binary matches the source, and they do not read the source for bugs. The check also depends on the keys: if the keys of the builders are not independent of the project, the attestations are weaker than they appear. Finally, a reproducible build is expensive to do, and most users will not do it; they rely on the signatures of the few that do, which is a delegation of trust, though one that can be checked by any user who is willing to spend the time.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Package registry

items.head: What it is
items.body: A package registry is a public service where the authors of a programming language's libraries publish them, so that others can install them by name and version.

rows: [(n, e['registry'], e['latest']) for n, e in j['entries'].items() if e['registry'] in ('PyPI', 'crates.io')]

items.body: Each registry has an interface that answers a request with a document, usually in the JSON format, listing a library's versions and times, and the script of the chapter's evidence reads the latest version and its date from it.

slides.notes:
The registry is the place to look when choosing a library, because it holds the facts that a list in a book cannot keep up to date. The book's list was written at one moment, and the registry shows what has happened since: whether the library still publishes releases, how recent the latest one is, and which version a new project would get by default. A query to a registry is a computation on public data, which can be repeated by anybody, and it replaces an impression such as the library seems abandoned with a date.

The date of a registry entry is the date of the registry's record and may differ from the date of the work: the NuGet listing used here gives only the list of versions, so the entry for NBitcoin has the latest version 10.0.14 and no date, and the chapter makes no claim about its age. A recent release also does not mean that a library is correct, secure or maintained for the use the reader has in mind. The registries themselves are trusted intermediaries, and an install from a registry is an act of trust of the same kind as the download of a release, though without the signatures the Bitcoin Core project provides.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Alternative toolkit

items.head: What it is
items.body: An alternative toolkit is a library, a client or even a full-node implementation, other than Bitcoin Core, that lets a programmer work with Bitcoin in a language of their choice.

rows: [(n, (q - datetime.date.fromisoformat(e['date'])).days) for n, e in j['entries'].items() if n in ('bcoin', 'python-bitcoinlib', 'btcd')]

items.body: To judge a toolkit with data, one reads from the registry the latest version and the date, from the project's documentation what version of Bitcoin Core it supports, and from its repository how recently it changed. The saved metadata of python-bitcoinlib states that its RPC interface should work with Bitcoin Core v24.0 or later, and the run of release 31.1 in this chapter confirms that for the calls tried (Todd, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

slides.notes:
A toolkit saves the programmer from writing the serialization, the hashing and the signing again. The wrapper library of the interface branch is one kind; the others on the list do more, such as building and signing transactions without a node. The choice among them matters because a bug in the code that serializes a transaction or computes a hash is a bug in the money handling of the program, and because a toolkit that no longer follows the rules of the network will fail at some upgrade.

Three limits apply to the figures. The registry shows the packages that carry a name, and the book's names of the projects do not always match the package names: BitcoinJS appears here as bitcoinjs-lib and Bitcore as bitcore-lib, and the choice of the package is the author's. The data are from one day, and the figures for age will be different when the query is repeated. And the book's list is a list of existing libraries and not a recommendation; the book itself says only that it lists some of the best libraries, clients and toolkits (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Semantics
slides.sub: The semantics branch connects the chapter to the course's wider theme, the meaning of data.
slides.notes:
A reader who has run a node knows why the node's answer is worth trusting: it is the answer of a program that verified the data itself. Chapter 2 introduced the provenance graph for describing where data came from, and the node is the clearest case of a source whose provenance can be stated in a sentence. The branch states it, and also shows how the JSON that the node returns can be turned into linked data by adding a context, which is a small step that makes the same text interpretable by programs that know nothing about Bitcoin.

The branch is met in the examples of this chapter, where the node's answers to the block and transaction commands are JSON texts whose keys the reader has to interpret. The standards involved are the JSON-LD 1.1 recommendation of the World Wide Web Consortium for the format and the same consortium's PROV ontology for provenance, and both were read for this chapter (World Wide Web Consortium, 2020) (Lebo et al., 2013).

slides.title: Linked Data

items.head: What this section covers
items.body: Linked data is a way of publishing data so that its parts can be referred to from other data. Each thing that is described, and each kind of property it can have, is given a global identifier, and statements are made by connecting identifiers; the JSON-LD specification describes the idea as being all about describing the relationships between different resources, which may be defined in different documents on the web or within the same document (World Wide Web Consortium, 2020). In this chapter the things are blocks, transactions and nodes, and the statements are the fields that the node returns.

slides.notes:
Shared identifiers are what lets data from different sources be combined without guessing. The specification of JSON-LD explains the problem with plain names: tokens such as name and homepage are ambiguous, and the solution is to use IRIs for unambiguous identification, so that developers do not accidentally step on each other's terms (World Wide Web Consortium, 2020). The same argument applies to the Bitcoin data: the word hash in one program's output may mean the hash of a block and in another's the hash of a transaction including its witness, as the chapter's own transaction decoding showed.

Linked data does not make data true. It makes data interpretable, and what a statement says about the world is still up to the source of the statement. For Bitcoin, the truth of a statement about a block comes from the verification the node performed, not from the identifiers used to publish it, and that is why the verified data concept is placed in this group beside the technical ones.

Concepts in this section: Verified data, JSON-LD context, IRI.

slides.title: Verified data

items.head: What it is
items.body: Verified data is data that the party using it has checked against the rules instead of taking on someone's word.
