items.body: The chain of verification has a precise shape.

slides.notes:
The property can be described in the vocabulary of provenance. The PROV ontology of the World Wide Web Consortium provides classes for representing and exchanging information about how data was produced (Lebo et al., 2013). It describes an entity as a thing, physical, digital or conceptual, an activity as something that occurs over a period of time and acts upon or with entities, and an agent as something that bears some form of responsibility for an activity taking place (Lebo et al., 2013). In these terms the answer of a node is an entity that was generated by an activity, the verification, and attributed to an agent, the node that the reader runs.

Verified data is authoritative only for the party who verified it, and only to the extent of the node's software and its keeping of the data. A node that was altered, as the assurance group warned, would verify nothing. Verified data also does not travel: if the reader copies the node's answer into a document, the document's readers see only a number, and the provenance has to be added deliberately, for example with the vocabulary above, to tell them where the number came from.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: JSON-LD context
slides.sub: a context that maps JSON keys to IRIs

items.head: What it is
items.body: A JSON-LD context is the part of a JSON document that says what its keys mean.

rows: sorted((ctx[k], v) for k, v in doc.items())

items.body: In the specification the context sits under the key @context, either at the top of the document or inside an object, and its entries map a term to an IRI or to a map, which the specification calls an expanded term definition and which can add a type or other details (World Wide Web Consortium, 2020).

slides.notes:
A context lets the same document be read by a person as ordinary JSON and by a program as linked data. The specification gives the reason in a short phrase: the terms should expand to IRIs so that developers do not accidentally step on each other's terms (World Wide Web Consortium, 2020). For the data of a Bitcoin node this solves the ambiguity of names. The field hash of a block and the field hash of a decoded transaction are both called hash, and a context for each document can map the same key to different identifiers, so that a program combining the two sees that they are different properties.

Adding a context does not check anything. A context that maps height to an identifier for a different meaning would still be a valid context, so the quality of the vocabulary behind the identifiers is what matters, and a vocabulary of Bitcoin terms that the community has agreed on is not something this chapter relies on. The identifiers in the worked example are invented for the example and point to nothing. A context is also written against a particular set of keys, so it has to be revisited if the keys of the answer are renamed.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: IRI
slides.sub: a term expanded to an IRI

items.head: What it is
items.body: An IRI, short for internationalized resource identifier, is a global name written like a web address.

items.head: How it works
items.body: An IRI is made of parts, in the form of a scheme such as https, a path, and optionally a query and a fragment, which is the part after the symbol #. In a vocabulary, the part before the fragment names the vocabulary and the fragment names the term, so that many terms share one address.

slides.notes:
Identity is the foundation of linking: two documents can only be about the same thing if they use the same name for it. The specification says that IRIs are a fundamental concept of Linked Data, and that for nodes to be truly linked, dereferencing the identifier should result in a representation of that node (World Wide Web Consortium, 2020). Dereferencing means using the identifier to fetch something, so an IRI can serve at once as a name and as the address of a page that tells what the name means.

An IRI looks like a web address but need not lead anywhere, and the worked example's identifiers do not. Two IRIs that differ in one character name different things, so the capitalization and the final slash or fragment have to be exactly the same in every document that uses the identifier. A well-formed IRI is also not a promise that the thing is well defined: the quality of the definition is a matter of the people who maintain the vocabulary.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Computing foundations
slides.sub: The computing foundations branch collects the everyday vocabulary of programs and computers that the other branches use without stopping to explain it: bytes and bit shifts, times and random numbers, files and processes, libraries and databases
slides.notes:
Without this vocabulary the commands and logs of the chapter are noise: a log that says the signature cache has 16 MiB and the server was started with worker threads means nothing to a reader for whom a mebibyte, a cache and a thread are undefined. With it, each line of the output becomes a small fact that can be checked, and the reader can see why the project chose, say, a fixed number of bytes for a cookie or a database for the set of unspent outputs. The branch is deliberately plain, and each concept is tied to a line or a file of the chapter's own evidence.

The concepts are met in the start-up log, in the data directory, in the documentation of the build and in the source code that the chapter asks the reader to read. The branch has two groups. The first, representation, explains how information is written down: as bytes, as shifted bits, as a time, as a random value and in the Base64 text form. The second, systems, explains the places where programs run and meet each other: files and directories, processes, libraries, databases, platforms, network protocols and software tests.

slides.title: Representation

items.head: What this section covers
items.body: Representation is the group of concepts about how a program writes information down. Bitcoin Core's data is numbers and text, but on a computer both are sequences of bytes, and the same number can be written as bytes in two orders, as hexadecimal text or as Base64 text. A time is a number of seconds, a secret is a number that nobody can predict, and an amount is an integer that the program halves by moving its bits. The five concepts of the group are the byte, the bit shift, Unix time, the random number and Base64.

slides.notes:
Many apparent puzzles in the chapter are only questions of representation. Why does the hash of a block, printed by the node, look reversed compared with the bytes that were hashed? Why is the halving of the subsidy a shift and not a division? Why does the cookie file hold 64 characters when the cookie is 32 bytes? In each case the answer is that the same information has two representations, and that a program converts between them at a known point. A reader who sees this stops being confused by the conversions and can check them.

A representation is not the information. The text 1a6a93b3 and the four bytes it stands for are the same value, but a program that compares text with bytes will find them different, and a number written with its bytes in the other order is a different number. The concepts of the group therefore state, next to each representation, the rule for converting it and a computation that shows the conversion.

Concepts in this section: Bit and byte, Bit shift, Unix time, Random number, Base64.

slides.title: Bit and byte
slides.sub: a byte as two hexadecimal digits

items.head: What it is
items.body: A bit is a single binary digit, which is either 0 or 1. A byte is a group of eight bits, so it can take 256 different values, and a computer stores and sends information as a sequence of bytes.

items.head: How it works
items.body: The prefix mebi means a power of two, 2 to the power 20, and differs by about five percent from the million bytes of the prefix mega, which is why the file with the conversions uses its own names.

slides.notes:
Sizes in Bitcoin are given in bytes, and the chapter's figures only make sense when the unit is clear. A block header is 80 bytes, a hash is 32 bytes, which is 64 hexadecimal digits, a cookie is 32 random bytes, and the chapter's examples talk about caches of 16 MiB and a pruning target of 550 MiB. The size of a transaction in bytes decides how much of a block it takes, and the cost of running a node is counted in the bytes it stores and transfers, so a reader needs to move between the units easily.

Two confusions are frequent. A bit and a byte are different units, and a link speed given in bits per second must be divided by eight to give bytes. And a mebibyte is not a megabyte, so a figure in one unit must not be compared with a limit in the other without converting it; the download page of Bitcoin Core speaks of gigabytes, and the log speaks of mebibytes, so the reader should not expect the figures to match exactly.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Bit shift

items.head: What it is
items.body: A bit shift moves all the bits of an integer by a number of places. Shifting to the left by one place doubles the number and shifting to the right by one place halves it, with the bit that falls off the right end lost. Shifting by n places multiplies or divides by two to the power n.

items.head: How it works
items.body: The shift is exact as long as no non-zero bit falls off.

slides.notes:
Bitcoin's rules use shifts where one would otherwise write a division or a power. The function that computes the block subsidy starts from 50 coins and shifts the amount right by the number of halvings, and it first returns zero if the number of halvings is 64 or more, because the shift would then be undefined (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The compact form of the target in a block header multiplies a three-byte number by a power of 256, which is a shift left by a whole number of bytes. BIP 9 shifts a block's version right by 29 bits to see whether its top three bits are 001 (Wuille et al., 2015).

Shifts on integers of limited size have limits. The comment in the source says that the explicit check, which returns zero for 64 or more halvings, exists to force the block reward to zero when the right shift is undefined (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A shift whose result is undefined is a hazard of fixed-size integers, and the authors guard against it with a check. The python integers of the worked examples have no fixed size, so the examples of this chapter do not meet that limit, and the reader should not assume that every language behaves in the same way.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Unix time

items.head: What it is
items.body: Unix time is a way of writing a moment as a single number, the count of seconds since the start of 1 January 1970 in universal time.

Unix time counts seconds from one fixed moment, so the number is the same everywhere and a program turns it into a local date only when it prints it; the worked example prints its dates in universal time.

slides.notes:
A single number is easy to store, compare and calculate with. The consensus rules compare times of blocks with other times, such as the median time past of the previous blocks, and BIP 9 measures the start and the timeout of a deployment in the same unit (Wuille et al., 2015). A time in the header takes only four bytes, which is the reason the format was chosen, and the node can use ordinary integer comparison to enforce the rules about it.

The time of a block is a claim by the miner and not a measurement. The header of block 123456 has a time that is 2,906 seconds later than the median time past of its predecessors, and both numbers are correct for their purposes. A student who reads the time of a block as the exact moment of its creation will be wrong by minutes, and a student who forgets that a 4-byte unsigned number ends in February 2106 will misjudge how long the field can serve.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Random number

items.head: What it is
items.body: A random number, in the sense that security needs, is a value that an attacker cannot predict.

items.head: How it works
items.body: A source of randomness collects unpredictable events and mixes them into a state from which it produces output. The worked example calls the same function twice, and gets two different 32-character values, each the hexadecimal text of 16 random bytes.

slides.notes:
Every secret in the chapter is a random number whose strength is its length. The cookie is 32 random bytes, which is 256 bits, and the salt of a stored credential is 16 random bytes. If the source were predictable, the attacker could compute the secret instead of guessing it, and the interface, which has the power to spend from a wallet, would be open. Randomness is therefore a security matter, and the log of the node reports where it gets it.

A value that merely looks random, such as the output of a deterministic generator started from a known number, is not secure. The cookie or the salt must come from the secure source, and reusing the same value for two purposes would defeat it. Another trap is the length: a short random value is easy to guess even if the source is perfect, which is why the project chose 32 bytes for the cookie.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Base64

items.head: What it is
items.body: Base64 is an encoding that writes any sequence of bytes using only 64 printable characters. The standard that defines it describes the commonly used base 64, base 32 and base 16 encoding schemes, of which base 16 is the hexadecimal text of chapter 2 (Josefsson, 2006).

The standard describes the process: the encoding represents 24-bit groups of input bits as output strings of 4 encoded characters, formed by concatenating three 8-bit input groups and treating the 24 bits as four 6-bit groups, each of which is used as an index into an array of 64 printable characters, and special processing, the padding, is performed if fewer than 24 bits are available at the end (Josefsson, 2006).

slides.notes:
Many carriers of data, such as the headers of a web request, can hold only text. Base64 lets a program put arbitrary bytes into such a carrier. The Basic authentication scheme of HTTP, which Bitcoin Core accepts for its interface, transmits credentials as a user and a password separated by a colon, encoded using Base64 (Reschke, 2015).

The most common mistake is to treat the encoded text as protected. The standard of the Basic scheme itself warns that it is not secure on its own and should be used with a secure system, since the user and the password are passed over the network as cleartext (Reschke, 2015). For Bitcoin Core this is the reason the project advises against exposing the interface over the public Internet, and the reason a cookie or a hashed credential is kept in a file with restricted access.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Systems

items.head: What this section covers
items.body: Systems is the group of concepts about where programs run and how they meet. A program lives in files in a directory, runs as a process with threads, uses libraries written by others, keeps data in a database, is built for a platform, talks to other programs through a protocol, and is checked by tests. All of these appear in the chapter, from the data directory and the daemon to the libraries and the unit tests of the source.

slides.notes:
Bitcoin Core is a large program, and the chapter shows a reader how to build it, run it and talk to it. Each of those activities touches one of the concepts of this group, and a reader who can name them can read the documentation of the project, for example the file that lists what the data directory contains or the notes on what each platform needs. The group also helps with the final part of the chapter, where the choice of a library or a node implementation depends on the language and the platform.

These are general concepts, and the explanations here only go as far as the chapter needs. A reader who wants more about operating systems or databases will find that each concept is the subject of a large field; the aim here is to be precise about the facts the chapter rests on.

Concepts in this section: File and directory, Process and thread, Software library, Database, Platform, Network protocol, Software testing, Programming language.

slides.title: File and directory
slides.sub: the path of the cookie file

items.head: What it is
items.body: A file is a named piece of stored data, and a directory is a place that holds files and other directories, so that names form a tree.
The directory tree is resolved from the top: to find the cookie, the system reads the top directory to find lotsofspace, reads that to find bitcoin, and reads that to find .cookie.

slides.notes:
Almost everything that Bitcoin Core keeps is a file in a directory, and the documentation of the project describes the layout. The data directory of the node holds the blocks, the chain state, the log, the configuration file and the cookie, and the reader must know which of them can be deleted, which must be backed up and which must be protected from other users. A path is also how the node is told where to put its data, with an option that names a directory.

A path is relative or absolute, and a relative path depends on the directory the program was started in, which is a common cause of a program not finding its configuration. The project's documentation gives a different default location of the data directory for each of the three common systems, so a path that works on one machine is not a path that works on another.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Process and thread

items.head: What it is
items.body: A process is a program in execution: the computer loads the program, gives it an area of memory of its own and runs it.
The operating system schedules processes and threads onto the processor cores, and gives each process its memory, so that the memory use of a node is the sum of what its parts request.

slides.notes:
The distinction explains several facts about a running node. The daemon of the chapter is a single process that runs for days. Within it, the log of the book says that script verification uses 3 additional threads and that the interface started 4 worker threads, while the current log reports 16 worker threads, so that the node can check signatures and answer requests in parallel (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The project's documentation presents the split of the program into several processes as a gain in isolation (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

A thread does not make a program faster in every case, and more threads use more memory. For a reader the practical rule is that the number of threads, like the cache sizes, is a setting with a default, and the default of one release is not the default of another, as the two logs, with 4 and 16 worker threads, show.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Software library and Database

items.head: Software library
items.body: A software library is a collection of ready-made code that other programs call. The program does not copy the code into its own text; it names the library and uses its functions.
A library is used in one of two ways.

items.head: Database
items.body: A database is a store of data organised so that a program can find and change particular items quickly and safely. Two kinds appear in the chapter.

slides.notes:
Libraries make large programs possible and are also a source of risk. The build notes of Bitcoin Core list the libraries that must be installed before a build, such as the Boost libraries for general C++ code, SQLite for the wallet, ZeroMQ for messaging and Cap'n Proto for communication between processes (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Each of them is code that the project did not write and that guards money all the same, which is why the project documents its dependencies and offers a way to build them from source.

A library is trusted by the program that uses it. A flaw in a library affects every program that includes it, and a library that is no longer maintained, like the toolkits that the registry data of the ecosystem branch shows to be old, can fail when the rules of the network change. The reader should therefore ask of a library, as of a program, where it comes from and who looks after it.

---

A node must look up the unspent output that a new transaction spends, without reading the whole chain, and must do so for every input of every transaction. A database makes this lookup quick and, as SQLite's own summary of its features puts it, offers ACID transactions, even after power loss (SQLite, 2026). The same need arises for a wallet, which keeps keys, descriptors and transactions that it must never lose.

A database is not the chain. The chain state is derived from the blocks, and the help text of the node describes the option -reindex-chainstate as wiping the chain state and rebuilding it from the block files on disk (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Also, the word transaction means two different things in this chapter, a transfer of bitcoin and an atomic change of a database, and the two must not be mixed up.

slides.title: Platform

items.head: What it is
items.body: A platform is the kind of computer a program is built for.

rows: sorted({m.group(1) for n in names for m in [re.match(PLATFORM_D1, n)] if m})

items.head: How it works
items.body: The worked example extracts the platform name from each file name of the checksum list and finds eight.

slides.notes:
The user has to choose the right file, and the builder has to build one for each. The names combine, by their form, the processor family at the start with the operating system after it: x86_64-linux-gnu names the x86_64 family with Linux, arm64-apple-darwin the arm64 family with the system of Apple's computers, whose name in the book is macOS, and win64 names Windows on a 64-bit processor. The download for the wrong platform will not run, and the checksum list is organised by these names so that a user can find the line for the file they have.

The word platform is used loosely. In the first chapter it was used for kinds of wallet, such as desktop and mobile, and here it means the processor and the operating system. A program built for a platform may depend on features of the operating system, such as the way it handles files or the network, which is one more reason to test on each of them.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Network protocol

items.head: What it is
items.body: A network protocol is an agreement between programs about what messages look like and in what order they are sent.
A connection starts with the client opening a channel to the address and the port, over which the two sides exchange the messages of the protocol.

slides.notes:
The protocols decide who can talk to the node and how. The interface of the chapter uses JSON-RPC messages carried by HTTP, and the specification of JSON-RPC says that it is independent of the transport, so that the same messages may travel within a process, over sockets or over HTTP (JSON-RPC Working Group, 2013). The network of nodes uses its own protocol, whose spreading of data chapter 2 described as gossiping, and the network information of a node reports a protocol version, 70016 in the book's example (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A protocol says nothing about trust. HTTP in the form used here sends the credentials as cleartext, so the interface should not be reached over an open network, and the evidence node bound the interface to 127.0.0.1, which is why the chapter treats opening the port to the network as the largest risk. Two programs that speak the same protocol may also differ in the version they support, as the protocol version in the network information shows.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Software testing

items.head: What it is
items.body: A software test is a small program that runs another program, or a part of it, on chosen inputs and checks that the result is the expected one.

items.cap: program SoftwareTesting, lines 1 to 3 of 3, run under Python 3.14.4

slides.notes:
The README itself gives the reason: testing and code review is the bottleneck for development, and this is a security-critical project where any mistake might cost people lots of money (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The software holds no money itself, but it decides which transactions are valid, and a bug in the rules could split the network or let a transaction through that should be refused. For a reader, the tests are also a source of runnable examples of the behaviour that the chapter describes.

Passing tests do not prove that a program is correct; they show that it behaves as expected on the cases that someone thought of. The project's own statement that review is the bottleneck acknowledges that tests and review complement each other. A reader who relies on a release should also remember that the release was tested on the platforms of the project's continuous integration, and not necessarily on the reader's own.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Programming language

items.head: What it is
items.body: A programming language is a formal notation in which a person writes the instructions of a program, together with the rules that give each form of writing its meaning.

items.head: How it works
items.body: A program in a compiled language, such as C++, is translated before it runs into machine instructions for one platform, which is why a release has an archive for each platform.

slides.notes:
The choice of language shapes what a program can do and what its authors have to take care of. The files of Bitcoin Core's source tree that the chapter reads have the ending cpp or h, such as validation.cpp and pow.cpp, which is the C++ in which the node is written, and the build notes warn that C++ compilers are memory-hungry (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Python appears where convenience matters more than speed: the project's README says that its regression and integration tests are written in Python, and the helper script for credentials, rpcauth.py, is a python program (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

A language is not a library and not a platform, although the three are often mentioned together. Knowing the language of a toolkit does not tell the reader whether the toolkit is maintained or correct, which is a question for the package registry and the project, as the ecosystem branch shows. And the same idea looks different in each language: the shift, the byte and the hash of the earlier concepts exist in all of them, but their spelling and limits differ, so a result computed in python is a statement about the rule and not about how another language would write it.

Source: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 3, Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

items.q: What question do the four concepts of the verification group answer together?
options: How a miner decides which transactions go first inside a new block
How much disk space a node needs before its first download can finish
How a participant can be sure that what the software enforces is what Bitcoin requires
How a user can recover coins after losing the file that holds the keys

items.q: Why does a user who runs a full node have to trust less than one who asks another server?
options: The node is run by the miner of the block, so the miner no longer needs trust
The node checks blocks against public rules, so only the software and the rules need trust
The node encrypts every payment, so no outside party can see any amount
The node keeps the user's keys offline in a separate device, so a stolen password cannot move coins

items.q: What property makes a change to the consensus rules a soft fork?
options: Older nodes reject every block that newer nodes create, so all of them must upgrade at once
Newer nodes may reject blocks that older nodes accept, but never the other way round
The change is voted on by users, and the network splits if the vote fails
Old and new nodes accept exactly the same blocks, so no new rule is enforced

slides.notes:
Answers. (1) C - The group names the program that checks the rules, the model program, the documents that record the rules and the soft fork that changes them.  (2) B - A user who relies on someone else's server has to trust that server, while a full node verifies everything itself and the rules are public.  (3) B - The book defines the property: nodes with the change must not accept blocks that nodes without it would consider invalid.

Every option here is a statement the chapter can judge: there is no filler option, so a student who guesses has to choose between four claims about Bitcoin and defend one.

Nakamoto revealed an identity in a statement signed with the first key

They apply only to nodes that run on a metered connection
They are orders of magnitude that change from year to year and are not constants
They were measured on test networks and not on the main network

The set of unspent outputs first, then the blocks that created each output
Only the latest blocks first, then older ones whenever a peer asks for them
Headers first, to find the chain with most proof of work, then the blocks, validated on arrival

options: It can no longer hand old blocks to other nodes
It stops verifying new blocks and trusts the peers that send them
It loses the set of unspent outputs and rebuilds it for each payment
It must connect to a single trusted peer that stores the full chain

items.q: Why does a node keep the set of unspent outputs instead of searching the whole history?
options: The set stores every wallet balance, so one lookup gives the amount owned
The history is deleted again once the node has downloaded it, so only the set remains
The set holds all signatures, so scripts never have to be run a second time
To check a transaction it only has to know whether each output it spends is in the set

items.q: Why do the printed build commands of Mastering Bitcoin fail on a current source tree?
options: Release 29.0 migrated the build from Autotools to CMake, and the tree has no autogen.sh
The project left GitHub, so the cloning command of the book finds nothing
The source is now written in Python only, so no compiler is needed for the build of the program
Git no longer allows a release tag to be checked out in a detached state

slides.notes:
Answers. (7) A - A pruned node still verifies, but it deleted old blocks and so cannot serve them to other nodes.  (8) D - A node does not need to search the history: it needs to know whether each output being spent is in the set, which is much smaller than the chain.  (9) A - The commands belong to a build system that was replaced in release 29.0, and the current tree has a top-level CMakeLists.txt and no autogen.sh.

Every option here is a statement the chapter can judge: there is no filler option, so a student who guesses has to choose between four claims about Bitcoin and defend one.
